title: The Tale of the Old Woman and the King
summary: During an imperial procession through the outskirts of Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya’s ceremonial tusker grew excited by the sound o...
keywords: the tale of the old woman and the king
full_text:
During an imperial procession through the outskirts of Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya’s ceremonial tusker grew excited by the sound of festival drums. The elephant broke away from the procession road and trampled straight through the small vegetable patch belonging to an impoverished widow named Parvatamma, crushing her entire season's crop of brinjals, gourds, and lentils.

The royal officers tossed the old woman two copper coins and rode away, ignoring her weeping.
Heartbroken, Parvatamma came to Tenali Raman’s home, crying that her grandchildren would starve.

Tenali comforted her: 'Mother, King Krishnadevaraya is a righteous king whose officers have acted with callous arrogance. Come with me to the palace tomorrow.'

The next morning, while the King was holding public audience, Tenali entered leading the weeping old woman.
Tenali bowed:
'Maharaj, a grave dispute has arisen regarding a tenant farmer who damaged an imperial property. The court desires to know: if a careless subject destroys a neighbor's livelihood, what is the lawful punishment?'

The King replied with firm authority:
'The law of Vijayanagara is clear! The offender must restore the damage tenfold, and must personally help restore the ruined field with his own hands!'

Tenali smiled with solemn reverence:
'Jahanpanah, your decree is righteous.
Yesterday, your imperial ceremonial tusker trampled through this widow's only vegetable field, destroying her entire year's sustenance, while your officers tossed her two coppers!
According to your royal verdict just spoken, the Emperor must restore her crop tenfold, and provide personal labor to repair her field!'

The courtiers gasped at Tenali’s audacity.
King Krishnadevaraya’s face flushed red, but the Emperor possessed genuine greatness of spirit.
He stood up from his golden throne and descended to the marble floor:
'Tenali is right. A king’s elephant cannot be above the law that protects the poor.'

The King ordered the royal treasury to pay Parvatamma one hundred gold dinars—tenfold the value of her crop—and granted her permanent title to five fertile acres with canal irrigation.
Furthermore, to demonstrate humility before his subjects, the King sent a royal team of bullocks and palace gardeners to plow and sow her new field completely!

Parvatamma blessed the King with tears of joy.
The people of Vijayanagara cheered their Emperor’s justice, while Tenali showed that true loyalty holds a mirror of righteousness before power.
moral: Sovereigns must remember that the humblest citizen’s bread is sacred; royal power owes full restitution for unintended damage.

title: Tenali and the Cursed Village
summary: A delegation of terrified village elders from Ramapuram, three leagues south of Vijayanagara, arrived at the court pleading for royal hel...
full_text:
A delegation of terrified village elders from Ramapuram, three leagues south of Vijayanagara, arrived at the court pleading for royal help:
'Maharaj, our village has been struck by an evil demon’s curse!
Whoever drinks from our central stone well falls victim to burning stomach fevers, shivering, and vomiting!
Two astrologers have performed animal sacrifices and burned black incense, but the curse grows stronger! We must abandon our ancestral village!'

King Krishnadevaraya was about to order the village evacuated when Tenali Raman spoke:
'Maharaj, demons rarely live in clean stone wells. Allow me to visit Ramapuram and investigate this curse.'

Tenali rode to Ramapuram accompanied by two royal apothecaries.
He inspected the 'cursed' well.
The stone well was situated in a low hollow near the village perimeter.
Tenali walked around the surrounding area:
Just fifty yards uphill from the well was a large commercial leather tannery operated by a careless merchant, along with an open pile of rotting animal hides and refuse!
Tenali noticed that recent summer rains had washed the toxic, rotting runoff from the tannery down the slope, where it was seeping through the porous limestone rocks directly into the groundwater of the well!

Tenali gathered the villagers:
'Look, brothers! Your curse does not come from demons of the underworld, but from the dirt and rotting waste of yonder tannery!
When you allow filth to soak into your drinking water, the fever is born of your own neglect!'

Tenali immediately organized the villagers into work teams:
They shut down the tannery and moved it two miles downriver;
They thoroughly drained and cleaned the stone well, scrubbing its walls with lime and burning charcoal;
They treated the water with fresh lime and clearing-nuts (*Strychnos potatorum*);
And they constructed a high stone wall and drainage ditch around the wellhead to divert all surface runoff.

Within three days, the water was sparkling clear, cool, and sweet.
Those who drank it suffered no fevers, and the sick recovered with simple herbal teas.

The villagers rejoiced, celebrating Tenali as their savior.
Tenali smiled:
'Remember, friends: cleanliness is the truest prayer, and clean water is the greatest blessing. When disease strikes, look to your drains and wells before you blame the stars!'
moral: Superstition blames phantoms for human neglect; scientific hygiene and sanitation cure what spells cannot.

title: Tenali and the Talking Mynah
summary: Two arrogant and envious courtiers, Lord Malhar and Lord Vasudev, frequently gathered in the palace garden pavilions to whisper malicious...
full_text:
Two arrogant and envious courtiers, Lord Malhar and Lord Vasudev, frequently gathered in the palace garden pavilions to whisper malicious gossip, mocking King Krishnadevaraya’s poetry and scheming against his ministers.
Knowing that walls have ears, they conducted their treasonous whispers inside a secluded arbor covered in thick passionflower vines.

Tenali Raman discovered their secret meeting spot.
Instead of denouncing them directly without proof, Tenali acquired a brilliant hill mynah bird—a creature renowned for its uncanny ability to mimic human voices with flawless accuracy.

For two weeks, Tenali secretly placed the mynah’s wicker cage hidden within the dense passionflower foliage above the courtiers' stone bench.
Whenever Malhar and Vasudev sat below, sipping wine and mocking the King, the clever bird listened quietly, absorbing their exact words, vocal tones, and chuckles.

During the grand royal festival of Vasantotsava, King Krishnadevaraya held court in the open garden pavilion before hundreds of dignitaries.
Tenali Raman entered carrying the mynah in an ornate golden cage covered with a silk veil.
'Maharaj,' announced Tenali, 'I have brought a remarkable royal songbird from the Nilgiris that can recite the most candid, unrehearsed poetry composed in your palace gardens!'

The King smiled: 'Let us hear its song, Tenali!'

Tenali pulled away the silk veil.
The mynah cocked its head, looked directly at Lord Malhar and Lord Vasudev sitting in the front row, and began reciting in Lord Malhar’s unmistakable, pompous nasal voice:
*‘The King thinks he is a poet, but his verses sound like an ox groaning in a ditch! He-he-he!’*

The court froze in stunned silence! Lord Malhar turned white as linen!
Then the mynah switched seamlessly to Lord Vasudev’s shrill, squeaky voice:
*‘Aye, Malhar! And when the treasury sends gold to the army, we shall pocket our twenty percent as usual before the fool notices!’*

The entire assembly gasped in horror!
Lord Vasudev collapsed onto the carpet in terror, while Lord Malhar began babbling incoherent apologies.
The King’s eyes blazed with righteous anger:
'Guards! Arrest these traitors! Audit their accounts immediately!'

The imperial audit revealed massive embezzlement by both courtiers. Their estates were confiscated, and they were sentenced to hard labor on the frontier fortresses.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, thy talking bird has unmasked treason that fifty spies could not detect!'
The clever mynah was appointed the official mascot of the imperial gardens, fed on sweet figs and almonds for the rest of its days.
moral: Those who whisper malicious slander behind closed doors are caught by the innocent mirrors of nature.

title: Tenali and the Three Thieves
summary: While traveling through the dense Nallamala forest on state business, Tenali Raman’s solitary bullock cart was ambushed by three fierce h...
full_text:
While traveling through the dense Nallamala forest on state business, Tenali Raman’s solitary bullock cart was ambushed by three fierce highwaymen: Bhima, Somu, and Kalu.
They dragged Tenali from the cart, demanding his gold.

Tenali remained completely composed. He looked at the three robbers and sighed:
'Brothers, you have stopped me on the wrong day. I carry only fifteen gold coins in my leather pouch.
However, if you spare my life, I will show you where an enormous treasure is buried: a brass chest containing ten thousand gold dinars, hidden by a merchant beneath the roots of the ancient banyan tree by the river!'

Greed ignited in the highwaymen’s eyes. They marched Tenali to the banyan tree and dug into the earth.
To their amazement, their iron spades struck a real iron chest that Tenali had discovered on an earlier journey!
Inside were hundreds of gleaming ancient silver and copper coins!

The three bandits cheered wildly.
Tenali said: 'Brothers, you have labored hard. It is noon, and you must be starving.
Let one of you run to the village tavern a mile away to buy roast meat and bread, while the other two guard the treasure.'

The youngest bandit, Kalu, volunteered and ran to the village.
As soon as he was gone, Bhima whispered to Somu:
'Why should we divide this treasure into three shares? When Kalu returns with the food, let us strike him down with our cudgels, and split the gold between the two of us!'
Somu agreed with a greedy grin.

Meanwhile, on his way back from the village, Kalu thought to himself:
'Why should I share the treasure with those two brutes? I will buy poison from the apothecary and mix it into the roasted meat! When they eat, they will perish, and the entire hoard will be mine!'

Kalu returned to the banyan tree carrying the poisoned food.
The moment he stepped into the clearing, Bhima and Somu leaped from the brush, striking Kalu down with their heavy cudgels!
Kalu collapsed dead upon the grass.

Laughing at their supposed cleverness, Bhima and Somu sat upon the iron chest and ravenously devoured the roasted meat.
Within ten minutes, the deadly poison took effect: both bandits clutched their stomachs, groaned in agony, and fell lifeless beside their victim!

Tenali Raman stepped out from the shade of the banyan tree, shook his head with sorrowful wisdom, and said:
'Greed digs its own grave, and malice poisons its own cup.'

Tenali loaded the iron chest onto his cart, drove to the nearest town, and surrendered the recovered treasure to the magistrate to build an orphanage, demonstrating that evil inevitably consumes itself.
moral: Thieves who unite through greed are easily divided and defeated by their own mutual suspicion.

title: Tenali and the Precious Ring
summary: While enjoying an evening boat ride upon the Tungabhadra River, Queen Tirumala Devi leaned over the gilded railing to watch the lotus blo...
full_text:
While enjoying an evening boat ride upon the Tungabhadra River, Queen Tirumala Devi leaned over the gilded railing to watch the lotus blossoms. Her ancestral emerald signet ring—a priceless gem engraved with the royal insignia of Vijayanagara—slipped from her finger and vanished into the swirling, deep currents!

Royal divers searched the riverbed for three days, but the rocky, murky bottom yielded nothing.
The Queen fell into deep sorrow, refusing to eat.
King Krishnadevaraya proclaimed a reward of one thousand gold coins to whoever could recover the ring.

Tenali Raman studied the river currents where the boat had been anchored.
He knew that predatory river fish, especially large catfish and carp, are attracted to shiny, glittering objects sinking through the water, often swallowing them whole.
He also knew that local fishermen cast their large drift-nets at that exact bend every dawn.

Tenali did not dive into the mud.
Instead, he took five hundred gold coins from his own savings and went to the main fish harbor at sunrise, just as thirty fishing smacks docked with their morning catch.

Tenali mounted a wooden crate and shouted in a booming voice:
'Listen, fishermen of Vijayanagara! By royal order, I purchase every single fish caught at the Golden Bend this morning!
Bring your baskets to my scale; I will pay double the market price in cash!'

The delighted fishermen brought forty baskets of fresh river fish to Tenali’s courtyard.
Tenali hired five trusted fishmongers, promising a silver coin for every belly cleaned, with one strict condition:
'Inspect the stomach of every fish with utmost care before washing!'

For three hours, the fishmongers cleaned the fish.
Suddenly, from the belly of a massive, thirty-pound river mahseer, a brilliant flash of green light illuminated the table!
The fishmonger cried out in amazement:
Inside the fish's stomach was Queen Tirumala Devi's emerald signet ring, completely undamaged and gleaming with peerless brilliance!

Tenali washed the ring in rosewater and carried it straight to the palace.
When the King and Queen saw the recovered heirloom, tears of joyous wonder filled their eyes!
The Queen rewarded Tenali with a diamond necklace, while the King distributed the forty baskets of cleaned fish to feed all the orphanages and hospitals of Vijayanagara.

The people celebrated Tenali’s brilliant deductive logic, marveling that while others looked into the mud, Tenali looked into the nets of nature.
moral: Careful inquiry and bold, unorthodox action recover what seemed irrevocably lost to the depths.

title: Tenali and the Mirror
summary: As King Krishnadevaraya approached his fiftieth year, he noticed silver strands appearing in his hair and subtle lines around his eyes. A...
full_text:
As King Krishnadevaraya approached his fiftieth year, he noticed silver strands appearing in his hair and subtle lines around his eyes. A melancholy gloom settled over the Emperor. He refused to look into mirrors, banished all grey-haired servants from his presence, and spent thousands of gold coins on charlatans who promised alchemical elixirs of perpetual youth.

The court ministers worried as state matters were neglected while the King bathed in herbal oils and brooded over his reflection.

Tenali Raman resolved to heal the King’s soul.
Tenali commissioned a master glassmaker to craft an extraordinary bronze hand mirror. The glass was polished with exceptional clarity, but around its ornate silver frame, Tenali had four miniature scenes carved in relief:
At the bottom: A young sprout breaking through the soil;
On the right: A blooming lotus in full summer glory;
At the top: A golden banyan tree laden with sweet fruit sheltering travelers;
On the left: A peaceful river flowing gracefully into the eternal ocean.

Tenali brought the mirror to the King's bedchamber:
'Maharaj, I have brought the Mirror of True Age, which reveals the eternal truth of royalty.'

The King hesitated, then looked into the glass.
He saw his silvering hair, his seasoned brow, and the lines of fifty years of leadership.
He frowned: 'Tenali, this mirror shows my aging face; why dost thou call it miraculous?'

Tenali knelt and pointed gently to the carved frame:
'Maharaj, look at the four seasons carved around your reflection:
When a man is twenty, he is like the green sprout—full of raw energy, but easily swayed by winds.
When he is thirty, he is the blooming lotus—dazzling, but preoccupied with his own splendor.
When he reaches fifty, Maharaj, he becomes the Golden Banyan Tree!
His silver hairs are the deep roots of experience; his lines are the branches of wisdom that shelter thousands of subjects from storms!
And in his twilight, he is the calm river that enriches the entire earth before merging with eternity.

Would Your Majesty trade the majesty of a sheltering banyan tree for the weak sprout of a youth who has never fought a battle or governed an empire?
Grey hair on a wise king is not a blemish; it is the silver crown of wisdom placed upon his head by heaven itself!'

Tears filled King Krishnadevaraya’s eyes as Tenali’s profound philosophical words touched his heart.
The heavy cloud of vanity and fear lifted from the Emperor's spirit.
He smiled, embracing Tenali with deep gratitude:
'Tenali, thou hast restored my dignity as a man and my purpose as a king!'

The King threw away the fraudulent youth potions, returned to the diwan with renewed energy, and governed his people with the ripe, loving wisdom of the Golden Banyan Tree.
moral: Accepting the natural passage of time with grace and wisdom brings true dignity that false youth cannot buy.

title: Tenali and the Hungry Brahmin
summary: In Vijayanagara lived a scholar named Bhimasena who had a monstrous, uncontrolled appetite. Whenever a wealthy citizen hosted a wedding o...
full_text:
In Vijayanagara lived a scholar named Bhimasena who had a monstrous, uncontrolled appetite. Whenever a wealthy citizen hosted a wedding or memorial feast, Bhimasena would push his way to the front, eating thirty sweet laddus, ten bowls of ghee payasam, and mountains of rice, until he could barely breathe!
One evening, after devouring an entire banquet at the Prime Minister’s mansion, Bhimasena collapsed upon the courtyard floor, clutching his bloated stomach, groaning in agonizing indigestion:
'Oh, my stomach! I am dying! The food is killing me! Call the physicians!'

The royal physicians prepared heavy doses of bitter castor oil and nauseating herbal pastes, but Bhimasena refused to swallow them, screaming in pain.

Tenali Raman stepped into the room with a smile:
'Step aside, learned doctors! I possess the ancient infallible remedy of Sage Charaka: the Medicine of the Three Miracles!'

Tenali instructed four servants to carry the groaning glutton into a quiet, airy room in his own house.
Tenali placed Bhimasena upon a firm wooden bench.
First Miracle: Tenali brought a large jug of pure warm water with a squeeze of fresh lime juice and a pinch of rock salt:
'Drink this slowly, friend. It will extinguish the fire in thy belly.'
Bhimasena drank, and the warm lime water eased his immediate cramps.

Second Miracle: Tenali bolted the room door from the outside, opened the barred windows to the fresh garden breeze, and announced:
'Now begins the sacred twenty-four-hour Fast of Absolute Silence!
No rice, no laddus, no sweetmeats! Only clean water until tomorrow sunset!'

Bhimasena shrieked and begged for food, but Tenali sat outside on the veranda reading witty stories aloud with his friends, laughing heartily.
Whenever Bhimasena groaned, Tenali shouted through the window:
'Laugh with us, Bhimasena! A hearty laugh shakes the liver, stimulates the digestion, and burns away thirty pounds of greed!'

For twenty-four hours, Bhimasena rested, fasted, drank warm water, and listened to laughter.
By the following evening, his bloated stomach had flattened, his cramps were gone, his fever had cooled, and his tongue was clean and pink!

Tenali unlocked the door and served him a modest, steaming bowl of light moong dal khichdi seasoned with cumin.
Bhimasena ate the simple khichdi, tears of genuine gratitude streaming down his cheeks:
'Tenali! Never in my life has any rich banquet tasted so delicious as this humble bowl of khichdi!'

Tenali smiled warmly:
'Food is medicine when taken with hunger and moderation, but it becomes poison when taken with greed. Remember: the stomach is an engine to serve thy mind, not a bottomless pit to bury thy dignity!'

Bhimasena was cured of his gluttony forever, becoming an advocate of healthy fasting and moderation throughout the city.
moral: Gluttony destroys health and self-respect; moderation and fasting are the truest medicine for body and soul.

title: Tenali and the Wooden Horse
summary: A boastful foreign carpenter and toy-maker named Shilpi Somappa arrived at King Krishnadevaraya’s court with an intricately carved, life-...
full_text:
A boastful foreign carpenter and toy-maker named Shilpi Somappa arrived at King Krishnadevaraya’s court with an intricately carved, life-size wooden horse painted in glittering gold and emerald lacquer.
Somappa claimed:
'Jahanpanah! This is no ordinary wooden toy! It is an enchanted "Celestial Flying Steed"!
Inside its belly is a complex mechanism of bronze gears and clockwork springs.
When the master pilot presses the secret silver peg behind its left ear, the horse will flap its mechanical wings, rise into the clouds, and fly across five hundred leagues in a single hour!
I offer this military marvel to Your Majesty for ten thousand gold dinars!'

King Krishnadevaraya and his generals were fascinated. The thought of an aerial warhorse that could fly over enemy fortress walls was intoxicating.
The King was on the verge of handing over the ten thousand gold coins when Tenali Raman spoke:
'Maharaj, this is indeed an extraordinary invention! Let us witness its flight before paying the gold.'

The carpenter began to stammer:
'Your Majesty, the mechanism is delicate; it requires an auspicious planetary alignment, which will not occur for six months! But if you pay the ten thousand coins now, I will complete the tuning!'

Tenali smiled with dazzling enthusiasm:
'Nonsense, Master Shilpi! The stars are in magnificent alignment today!
In fact, I shall pilot the flying horse myself!'

Tenali leaped onto the back of the wooden horse in the palace courtyard.
He grabbed the painted reins, found the silver peg behind the ear, and pressed it firmly!
Nothing happened. The heavy wooden horse remained completely stationary upon the stone tiles.

Tenali shouted: 'Fly, celestial steed! Rise into the clouds!'
He bounced up and down upon the wooden saddle, making loud whinnying sounds:
*‘NEIGH! CLOP-CLOP! FLY TO THE CLOUDS!’*
The horse did not move an inch.

Tenali then turned to the carpenter:
'Ah! Perhaps the horse requires its creator’s magical touch!
Master Shilpi, mount the horse behind me! We shall fly together from the top of the seven-story palace tower!
Guards, carry this wooden horse to the highest parapet of the fortress tower, so Master Shilpi can demonstrate its flight by jumping into the air!'

The carpenter turned pale as a corpse!
He threw himself onto his knees, trembling, clutching the King's feet:
'Mercy, Maharaj! Do not throw me from the tower!
The horse cannot fly! It is only hollow cedar wood and cheap iron springs! I forged the mechanism to swindle ten thousand gold coins from the treasury!'

The court erupted in laughter at the exposed fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya reprimanded the carpenter, sentenced him to build wooden benches for public schools for a year, and praised Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, thy willingness to test flight from the tower grounded a soaring swindler in an instant!'
moral: Charlatans who promise magical machines to fleece the royal treasury are easily exposed when asked to pilot their own inventions.

title: Tenali and the Village Headman
summary: The village headman of Bellary, a tyrannical official named Patel Basappa, ruled his district through fear and corruption. Whenever a poo...
full_text:
The village headman of Bellary, a tyrannical official named Patel Basappa, ruled his district through fear and corruption. Whenever a poor farmer needed his land deed stamped, or a dispute resolved, Basappa demanded heavy bribes in silver, sheep, and ghee.
To intimidate the peasants, Basappa had an iron chair in his office, boasting:
'I sit upon the Iron Throne of Authority! None can move me from this seat!'

A group of ruined farmers walked to Vijayanagara and fell at Tenali Raman’s feet, begging for deliverance.
Tenali assured them: 'Return home, brothers. Tomorrow, Patel Basappa shall find his iron throne uncomfortably warm.'

Tenali traveled disguised as a wealthy diamond merchant from Golconda, wearing embroidered silks and a velvet turban.
He entered Basappa’s office, carrying a heavy brass chest.
Tenali bowed:
'Revered Patel, I desire to purchase fifty acres of fertile land in your district. Here are five hundred gold coins as your "private consultation gift". But I must be certain: do you truly possess absolute, unshakeable authority in this village?'

Basappa’s eyes gleamed with greed at the sight of the gold:
'Absolute authority, noble merchant! I sit upon this iron chair, and my word is law! No power on earth can make me abandon this seat or change my decree!'

Tenali said: 'Prove it to me, Patel. Sit firmly upon your iron chair while I prepare the legal documents.'

While Basappa sat grinning greedily, Tenali gave a prearranged signal to four village blacksmiths waiting outside with long iron tongs.
The blacksmiths carried in large iron braziers filled with glowing red-hot charcoal, and placed them directly beneath the hollow base of Basappa’s iron chair!
Within minutes, the thick iron seat began to conduct the heat!

Basappa began to squirm: 'What are you doing, merchant? It feels warm!'
Tenali replied calmly, writing slowly with a quill:
'Patience, Patel! The legal ink requires warmth to dry properly! A man of unshakeable authority can surely endure a gentle warmth!'

As the iron seat grew scorching hot, Basappa shrieked in agony, leaped into the air like a scalded monkey, clutching his burnt buttocks, and danced wildly around the room!
*‘OUCH! MERCY! MY CHAIR IS ON FIRE!’*

Tenali threw open the doors:
Standing in the doorway were King Krishnadevaraya and the royal guards!
Tenali pointed at the dancing official:
'Look, Maharaj! The corrupt headman claimed that no power on earth could move him from his seat of authority.
Yet when the heat of justice is applied, even the most stubborn tyrant jumps like a frog!'

The King ordered an immediate audit of Basappa’s accounts: hundreds of confiscated farms were returned to the poor peasants, Basappa was stripped of his office, and the villagers celebrated Tenali Raman as their champion of justice.
moral: Corrupt officials who extort bribes from poor peasants are undone when their own unlawful gains are placed upon the scales of justice.

title: Tenali and the Lost Camel
summary: While traveling along the dusty highway between Hampi and Bellary, Tenali Raman and three companions were stopped by an agitated, weeping...
full_text:
While traveling along the dusty highway between Hampi and Bellary, Tenali Raman and three companions were stopped by an agitated, weeping camel merchant:
'Noble travelers, have you seen my lost camel? It wandered away from my caravan last night, carrying my life’s savings!'

Tenali had never seen the camel, but having observed the trail during his walk, he asked:
'Was thy camel blind in its right eye?'
'Yes, yes!' cried the merchant.
'Was it lame in its left hind leg?'
'By heaven, exactly!'
'Was it missing one upper front tooth?'
'Yes! You have seen it!'
'Did it carry a load of sweet honey on its left flank, and a load of fine wheat on its right?'
The merchant shouted with joy: 'You know everything! Where have you hidden my camel?'

When Tenali smiled and said: 'I have never laid my eyes upon your camel, nor do I know where it is now,'
the merchant flew into a rage, seized Tenali’s robes, and dragged him before King Krishnadevaraya, accusing him of camel theft and witchcraft!

The King turned to Tenali: 'Tenali, how couldst thou describe the beast and its cargo with such absolute precision if thou hast never seen it?'

Tenali bowed with serene composure:
'Maharaj, I used no witchcraft, only the eyes heaven gave me!
First: Along the road, the thorn bushes were cropped clean on the left side of the path, while the lush branches on the right side remained untouched. A beast with two healthy eyes feeds equally on both sides; therefore, it was blind in its right eye.
Second: The footprints of three hooves were deep and firm in the dust, while the left hind hoof dragged lightly, making an uneven groove, proving lameness.
Third: Where the camel bit into the wild shrubs, a small gap of two inches was left unbroken in the center of every bite mark, indicating a missing upper front tooth!
Fourth: Along the path, swarms of black ants were busy carrying fallen grains of wheat on the right side of the trail, while swarms of buzzing flies were feasting on sweet drops of honey on the left side!
A blind man could reconstruct the camel from such plain evidence!'

Just as Tenali finished his explanation, the palace watchmen arrived leading the lost camel, which had been found grazing peacefully in a nearby ravine, with its wheat and honey intact!

The merchant blushed with profound embarrassment, fell at Tenali’s feet, and begged forgiveness.
King Krishnadevaraya marvelled at Tenali’s brilliant forensic deduction, rewarding him with a purse of gold and advising his ministers to cultivate the art of observant reasoning.
moral: Keen observation of subtle natural tracks reveals truth with forensic certainty without witchcraft.

title: Tenali and the King of Thieves
summary: A notorious master burglar named Chora Raja (The King of Thieves) sent an insolent letter to Emperor Krishnadevaraya: 'Imperial King! You...
keywords: tenali and the king of thieves
full_text:
A notorious master burglar named Chora Raja (The King of Thieves) sent an insolent letter to Emperor Krishnadevaraya:
'Imperial King! Your palace guards are sleeping sheep, and your treasury locks are made of clay.
On the night of the full moon, I will break into the Royal Treasury Vault inside the innermost citadel, steal the Great Emerald of Vijayanagara, and leave a painted flower in its place!'

The King was outraged and doubled the palace guards. Three hundred armored soldiers surrounded the treasury, and the chief locksmith installed triple steel padlocks.
Yet the King remained anxious and called Tenali Raman.

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, a master thief does not break through walls guarded by spears; he walks through doors opened by greed. Let me prepare the trap inside the vault.'

Tenali had all the gold coins and emeralds removed from the central display table in the vault and locked in a secret subterranean safe.
In their place, in the center of the dark vault, Tenali placed an enormous, magnificent iron-bound chest made of seasoned teakwood. The chest lid was slightly ajar, revealing a glittering false diamond necklace resting on velvet.
Tenali himself climbed inside the chest, armed with a small copper horn and a net of strong hemp cord, pulling the lid down to leave a two-inch breathing crack.

At midnight, a subtle shadow slipped through the high ventilation skylight using a silk rope.
Chora Raja had bribed an outer groom to learn the guard patrol schedule!
Silently landing on the marble floor of the vault, the master thief chuckled at his easy entry.

Seeing the massive teakwood chest in the center of the room with the glittering necklace peeking out, Chora Raja’s eyes gleamed with greed.
He crept forward, lifted the heavy lid, and reached his hands inside to seize the necklace!

Instantly, two powerful hands shot out from the darkness inside the chest, grabbing Chora Raja’s wrists with an iron grip!
Before the stunned burglar could draw his dagger, Tenali threw the heavy hemp net over his head and blew a deafening blast on his copper horn:
*‘HONK-TOOT-TOOT!’*

Fifty royal guards burst into the vault with torches and spears!
Chora Raja was pinned to the floor, completely tangled in the net!

When the thief looked into the chest and saw Tenali Raman grinning back at him, he gasped in disbelief:
'Who art thou that sleeps inside a treasure chest?'
Tenali laughed, climbing out of the box:
'I am the keeper of greed's mousetrap!
Thou didst boast that no lock could keep thee out, but thou didst forget that a thief’s own greed locks him in from the inside!'

The King rewarded Tenali with the recovered emerald, and Chora Raja was imprisoned, ending the reign of the boastful burglar.
moral: Audacious criminals who boast that no lock can hold them are trapped by their own irresistible greed.

title: Tenali and the Pot of Gold at Rainbow End
summary: A gullible, greedy courtier named Somadatta was obsessed with old folklore tales of pots of gold buried where rainbows touch the earth. W...
keywords: tenali and the pot of gold at rainbow end
full_text:
A gullible, greedy courtier named Somadatta was obsessed with old folklore tales of pots of gold buried where rainbows touch the earth. Whenever a monsoon shower passed over Vijayanagara and a colorful rainbow arched across the sky, Somadatta would abandon his court duties, mount his horse, and gallop frantically across hills, streams, and muddy ditches, trying to reach the foot of the rainbow!
Every time, the rainbow receded into the distance, leaving Somadatta bruised, soaking wet, and covered in mud.

Yet Somadatta insisted: 'Yesterday I saw the rainbow touching the eastern hills! Next time, I will ride faster and seize the gold!'

King Krishnadevaraya, amused by the courtier’s folly, asked Tenali Raman to cure him.

Tenali went to Somadatta’s house with an ancient-looking parchment map:
'Friend Somadatta, thou hast been searching in the wrong place!
Rainbows are celestial bridges; they touch the earth only when the soil has been thoroughly tilled, turned, and aerated!
Look at this neglected five-acre field behind thy estate.
The ancient astrological map states that if thou diggest three feet deep across this entire field with a spade before the next rain, the next rainbow will deposit its pot of gold directly in the center!'

Somadatta’s eyes widened with greed: 'Is this true, Tenali?'
'Upon my honor!' affirmed Tenali. 'Grab a spade and dig!'

For two months, Somadatta, who had never done a day’s manual work in his life, went out at dawn with a spade.
He dug, turned the heavy soil, removed stones, broke clods, and channeled water ditches, sweating profusely, his soft hands blistering and then hardening into strong, capable palms.
He dug up every single foot of the five-acre field three feet deep!

When the field was completely tilled, Tenali visited him carrying two sacks of prime wheat seed:
'Now, Somadatta, to attract the rainbow’s golden light, scatter these golden seeds across the plowed soil!'
Somadatta eagerly sowed the wheat.

The monsoon rains arrived. The seeds sprouted, and within four months, the entire field became an ocean of rich, golden, heavy-eared wheat!
When the harvest was reaped and sold at the market, Somadatta received two hundred gold dinars in cash!

Somadatta stood holding his heavy purse of real gold coins, looking at his fertile land.
Tenali walked up to him with a warm smile:
'Where is the rainbow, Somadatta?'

Somadatta laughed heartily, wiping sweat from his brow:
'Tenali, the rainbow was in the sweat of my own brow!
I chased colored light across the clouds and found only mud. But when I put my spade into the earth, the true pot of gold sprouted from the soil!'

Somadatta was cured of his foolish superstition, becoming an industrious farmer and a respected counselor in the imperial court.
moral: Chasing illusory promises of effortless wealth leads to exhaustion; honest labor is the only true pot of gold.

title: Tenali and the Talking Drum
summary: A traveling mendicant named Kapila arrived in Vijayanagara displaying an enormous wooden festival drum (*mridangam*), decorated with peac...
full_text:
A traveling mendicant named Kapila arrived in Vijayanagara displaying an enormous wooden festival drum (*mridangam*), decorated with peacock feathers and silver bells.
He proclaimed to the crowds in the temple square:
'This drum was consecrated in the sacred forests of Dandaka!
When I strike the goatskin drumhead, it does not merely make rhythm; it speaks in human language, revealing secret sins, predicting fortunes, and declaring who should donate gold!'

Kapila struck the drum: *DUM-DUM-DUM!*
And indeed, from the hollow belly of the drum came a deep, booming voice:
*‘Woe to the miser who hoards silver! Blessed is he who drops ten gold coins into the holy bowl!’*

Terrified citizens dropped coins into the bowl. Several courtiers whispered that the drum possessed divine power.
King Krishnadevaraya was curious and invited the mendicant to perform in the royal diwan.

Tenali Raman inspected the massive drum. It was extraordinarily large—almost five feet long and three feet in diameter, mounted upon a heavy wooden cart draped in thick, hanging velvet cloths.
Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, allow me to examine this musical oracle.'

Tenali approached the drum, bowed with deep reverence, and said:
'O Miraculous Drum! What did I eat for breakfast this morning?'
The drum boomed: *‘Pounded rice and curd!’*
Tenali asked: 'What is hidden in my left sleeve?'
The drum boomed: *‘A gold ring!’*

Tenali nodded. He stepped back, reached into his pouch, and pulled out an iron tongs holding a glowing charcoal ember and a bundle of dried, pungent bird's-eye chili peppers!
Before the mendicant could move, Tenali lifted the small leather flap near the drum's tuning peg and dropped the smoking chilies straight into the drum's sound hole!

Within five seconds, a frantic, coughing, screaming commotion exploded from inside the drum!
*‘COUGH! ACHO0! HELP! I AM BURNING! LET ME OUT!’*

The front goatskin of the drum burst open from the inside, and out tumbled a scrawny young boy, rubbing his streaming eyes, coughing and sneezing violently on the carpet!
Behind him inside the hollow wooden cylinder was a small leather cushion and a bowl of water!

The mendicant fell to his knees in terror, begging for royal mercy.
He confessed that he had hidden his nephew inside the hollow drum to fleece gullible crowds with ventriloquism and acoustic tricks!

King Krishnadevaraya was outraged by the charlatan’s sacrilege.
He confiscated the mendicant’s ill-gotten wealth to build a public library, sent the boy to an honest apprenticeship, and praised Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, thy chili smoke has cleared the air of another fraudulent mystery!'
The court celebrated Tenali’s unwavering defense of reason and truth.
moral: Acoustic trickery that exploits public awe is exposed by inspecting the instrument itself.

title: Tenali and the Two Liars
summary: Two professional boasters from rival provinces, Shankara and Narayana, met at a festival in Vijayanagara and began competing over who cou...
full_text:
Two professional boasters from rival provinces, Shankara and Narayana, met at a festival in Vijayanagara and began competing over who could tell the most outrageous falsehood without blinking.
Shankara boasted:
'Last year, I planted a pumpkin seed in my garden. Within three days, it grew into an enormous pumpkin so colossal that three hundred cavalry soldiers pitched their tents inside it during a rainstorm!'

Narayana scoffed:
'That is nothing! My grandfather was a coppersmith who cast an enormous bronze cooking cauldron so vast that two thousand blacksmiths hammered inside it for twenty years, and the sound of the hammers on one side could not be heard on the other!'

Shankara frowned, suspicious:
'Narayana, why on earth would anyone cast such a ridiculous, impossible bronze cauldron?'

Narayana smirked:
'Why, Shankara? To cook your colossal pumpkin, of course!'

The surrounding crowd laughed, declaring Narayana the winner.
Puffed up with pride, the two boasters turned to Tenali Raman, who was standing nearby:
'Hey, Tenali! They say thou art the greatest wit in the empire. Canst thou tell a lie greater than ours?'

Tenali Raman shook his head with grave, solemn dignity:
'Alas, brothers! I cannot participate in your contest, for in all my forty years of life, I have never spoken a single lie, nor have I ever exaggerated by half a syllable!
Every word that passes my lips is pure, unblemished, absolute truth!'

The two boasters stared at Tenali in stunned silence.
Narayana cried: 'What? A court jester who has never spoken a lie in forty years? That is the most monstrous, impossible, colossal lie ever spoken in the history of the world!'

Tenali smiled with effortless brilliance:
'Aha! Then by your own unanimous admission, my lie is far greater than your pumpkin and your cauldron combined! Hand over the championship prize!'

The entire crowd roared with unstoppable laughter.
The two boasters blushed crimson, realized they had been completely outmaneuvered by Tenali’s razor-sharp paradoxical wit, surrendered their prize purse, and slipped away into the crowd, proving that boasting cannot withstand true intelligence.
moral: Outlandish boasting defeats itself when met with an even greater claim of absolute truth.

title: Tenali and the Scented Flower
summary: A foreign ambassador from the Far East arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting an extraordinary gift to King Krishnadevaraya: An...
full_text:
A foreign ambassador from the Far East arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting an extraordinary gift to King Krishnadevaraya:
An exquisite crimson lotus flower with thirty-two translucent petals, emitting a sweet, delicate fragrance of jasmine and sandalwood.
The ambassador proclaimed:
'Your Majesty! This is the legendary Eternal Lotus of the Eastern Isle!
It never withers, its petals never fade, and its fragrance endures through all four seasons! It is an immortal botanical marvel!'

The King was captivated by the flower's flawless symmetry and scent. He placed it in a crystal vase in the royal diwan, showing it proudly to all visiting kings.

Tenali Raman inspected the flower from a distance.
He noticed that while the palace gardens outside were teeming with honeybees, butterflies, and sunbirds, not a single living insect ever flew near the 'Eternal Lotus' in the crystal vase.

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, nature does not create flowers that never wither. Allow me to test this miracle.'

Tenali walked into the palace garden, caught three lively honeybees inside a small glass jar, and brought them into the audience hall.
Tenali stood in the center of the hall, opened the glass jar, and released the three bees!

The bees buzzed into the air.
They circled the hall, flew past the crystal vase, completely ignored the crimson 'Eternal Lotus', and flew straight out the open window toward a bed of common, fading marigolds in the garden courtyard!

Tenali smiled:
'Maharaj, bees are guided by the pure scent of real nectar; they know what is alive and what is dead.
Observe!'

Tenali took the 'Eternal Lotus' from the crystal vase, held it over a small oil lamp, and touched the flame to the edge of a petal.
Immediately, the petal melted into clear, liquid wax with a faint smell of burnt tallow!
The flower was an intricate sculpture made of colored beeswax and chemical perfumes, forged by an artisan to swindle royal honors!

The ambassador hung his head in shame, confessing the fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, thy bees have taught us that artificial flattery and painted wax can never equal the honest, living truth of nature!'
The King rewarded Tenali, learning that true beauty needs no fraudulent claims of immortality.
moral: Artificial imitations can mimic outward beauty, but only living nature possesses the sweet truth of life.

title: Tenali and the King's Lost Slipper
summary: King Krishnadevaraya possessed a pair of ceremonial slippers woven of golden threads and encrusted with Burmese rubies, gifted to him by ...
keywords: tenali and the king's lost slipper
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya possessed a pair of ceremonial slippers woven of golden threads and encrusted with Burmese rubies, gifted to him by his beloved queen on his coronation anniversary.
One morning, while the King was preparing for audience, one of the precious slippers disappeared from the royal dressing room.
The palace was thrown into turmoil: sentries were questioned, rooms were searched, and the Chief Chamberlain accused a poor sweep-girl of theft, threatening her with prison.

Tenali Raman arrived at the dressing room.
He examined the velvet rug where the slipper had been placed:
There were no signs of forced locks or footprints, but near the balcony curtain, Tenali noticed a small scrap of dried mutton bone and the faint imprint of wet canine paws on the marble tiles.

Tenali smiled: 'Chamberlain, release the sweep-girl. The thief walks on four legs, not two.'

Tenali knew that King Krishnadevaraya owned an affectionate hunting hound named Bhairava, who was often allowed to roam the palace terraces.
Tenali went to the royal kennels, fetched Bhairava on a leather leash, and brought him to the King’s dressing room.

Tenali held the King’s remaining ruby slipper before the hound’s nose:
'Smell it, Bhairava! Find its twin!'

The hound sniffed the leather and royal sandalwood oil, whined with excitement, wagged its tail, and bolted down the marble corridor!
Tenali, the King, and the guards followed the bounding dog across the palace gardens, down a secluded stone flight of stairs, and into the cool, shady royal stable yard.

Bhairava ran straight to an ancient, hollow neem tree, stuck his snout into a dark hollow between the roots, and began barking with triumphant joy!
Tenali reached into the hollow:
Out came the King’s embroidered ruby slipper, completely undamaged, resting beside three old bones and an old leather ball!

The hound had found the soft, scented slipper, carried it off as a prized toy, and buried it in his secret cache!

King Krishnadevaraya laughed with immense relief and joy, patting the happy hound:
'Bhairava is our thief!'
The sweep-girl was exonerated and rewarded with a bag of gold coins for her distress, while Tenali showed that patient observation and trusting nature’s instincts solve puzzles without shedding innocent tears.
moral: A loyal dog’s keen instinct and patient tracking solve mysteries where human eyes wander blind.

title: Tenali and the Wicked Astrologer
summary: A gloomy, manipulative court astrologer named Bhairava Shastri, who sought to dominate King Krishnadevaraya through fear, arrived at the ...
full_text:
A gloomy, manipulative court astrologer named Bhairava Shastri, who sought to dominate King Krishnadevaraya through fear, arrived at the court with a dark, ominous parchment.
He prostrated himself before the throne, trembling with theatrical dread:
'Alas, Emperor Krishnadevaraya! The stars have aligned in a catastrophic conjunction!
Saturn and Mars have entered your house of life!
The planetary omens reveal that within thirty days, Your Majesty shall suffer an incurable, fatal affliction—unless you perform an imperial penance, surrender your royal signet ring to the temple council, and donate fifty thousand gold coins to my astrological academy!'

King Krishnadevaraya, devout and fearful of celestial wrath, turned pale. A heavy dread gripped the Emperor’s heart, and he fell into despair.

Tenali Raman stepped forward, his eyes flashing with sharp indignation at the charlatan’s cruel manipulation.
Tenali bowed to the King:
'Maharaj, before we surrender the empire’s treasury and signet ring, let us verify the infallible accuracy of the Pandit’s astrological foresight.'

Tenali turned to the astrologer, holding a sharp iron stylus in his hand:
'Revered Astrologer, your knowledge of planetary movements across the heavens is truly astonishing.
Tell me: does your chart reveal the exact hour, minute, and manner of your own death?'

The astrologer, eager to demonstrate total mastery over fate, puffed out his chest and boasted:
'Of course! My celestial horoscope is completely charted!
I am destined to live for another forty years in robust health, dying peacefully in my sleep at the ripe age of ninety-two, surrounded by my grandchildren!'

The moment the words left the astrologer’s lips, Tenali Raman drew the King’s ceremonial scimitar from its scabbard with a lightning flash of steel!
He placed the cold, razor-sharp blade gently against the astrologer’s trembling throat!

Tenali smiled with cold, terrifying amusement:
'Maharaj! Order the executioner to take this scimitar and sever this man’s head this very second!
If he dies right now on this carpet at the age of fifty-two, his horoscope was a fraudulent lie, and Your Majesty has nothing to fear from his thirty-day prophecy!
And if his horoscope was true, the sword will magically turn to flowers, so he has nothing to lose!'

The terrified astrologer shrieked in horror, fell to the floor, wet his robes in absolute panic, and babbed frantically:
'Mercy, Tenali! Mercy, Your Majesty! Do not strike!
My horoscope was a lie! The stars predicted no doom!
I forged the prophecy to terrify the King into granting gold and influence to my academy!'

King Krishnadevaraya sprang to his feet, his fear instantly transformed into righteous fury and profound relief!
The King ordered the fraudulent astrologer stripped of all titles and banished from Vijayanagara forever.
The Emperor embraced Tenali Raman with tears of gratitude:
'Tenali, thy fearless wit has broken the chains of fear that bound my spirit!'
The court celebrated Tenali as the champion of courage, demonstrating that superstition vanishes when confronted by bold reason.
moral: Charlatans who predict the doom of others to manipulate power are undone when asked about their own fate.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 72
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, pleased by the gentle touch and pleasant conversation of his personal royal barber, an illiterate man named Keshava...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, pleased by the gentle touch and pleasant conversation of his personal royal barber, an illiterate man named Keshava, made a whimsical announcement in the royal diwan:
'Keshava has served my head with such delicate skill that I have decided to honor him with the highest title of the realm!
I decree that Keshava shall be appointed Chief Royal Scholar of the Academy, with a salary of three hundred gold coins, and all the court pandits must bow before his wisdom!'

The court scholars were deeply humiliated, but terrified of contradicting the Emperor’s absolute command.
They appealed secretly to Tenali Raman.

Tenali smiled: 'Fear not, revered scholars. Tomorrow, we shall see how easily royal decrees can transform nature.'

The next morning, while King Krishnadevaraya was riding toward the river for his morning worship, he saw an extraordinary sight on the riverbank:
Tenali Raman was standing in the water with a scrawny, black street dog.
Tenali was vigorously scrubbing the dog with a rough stone, rubbing fragrant sandalwood paste into its fur, and chanting Sanskrit mantras at the top of his voice!

The King stopped his horse in astonishment:
'Tenali! What on earth are you doing to that dirty street dog in the sacred river?'

Tenali bowed with solemn respect:
'Jahanpanah! I am performing the Sacred Rite of Equine Transformation!
I am washing this street dog with holy water and sandalwood to turn it into a magnificent, pedigree Arabian warhorse for Your Majesty’s cavalry!'

The King stared at Tenali as though he had lost his mind:
'Tenali, art thou mad? No amount of scrubbing, sandalwood, or chanting can ever turn a dog into a horse! Nature cannot be changed by wishful washing!'

Tenali looked up at the King with piercing, sparkling wit:
'Indeed, Your Majesty! If no amount of scrubbing can turn a dog into a horse, how can a single royal decree turn an illiterate barber into a Chief Scholar of the Academy?
Scholarship requires decades of disciplined study, contemplation, and learning. When a king awards academic titles based on flattery rather than merit, he makes a mockery of learning and disgraces his empire!'

King Krishnadevaraya felt the sharp sting of truth in Tenali’s brilliant analogy.
He burst into appreciative laughter, revoked the barber’s academic appointment, and instead rewarded Keshava with a generous gift of gold and a comfortable house for his barber services.
The scholars cheered Tenali, who preserved the integrity of learning through the power of satire.
moral: True scholarship is earned through diligent study, not through royal decrees or superficial titles.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 73
summary: A cunning alchemist named Rasavadi Someshwar arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, claiming he had discovered the legendary Philosopher’s...
full_text:
A cunning alchemist named Rasavadi Someshwar arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, claiming he had discovered the legendary Philosopher’s Stone (*Sparshamani*).
Before the King and the ministers, he produced a heavy iron rod.
He dipped the tip of the rod into a bubbling crucible of sulfur and mercury, chanted a secret mantra, and pulled it out:
To the astonishment of the King, the tip of the rod had turned into glittering, solid twenty-four-karat gold!

The King was dazzled: 'Someshwar, canst thou turn all the iron in our armory into gold?'
The alchemist bowed: 'Easily, Your Majesty! But the alchemical reaction requires a catalytic seed fund: you must provide me with five thousand gold coins to purchase the rare Himalayan herbs necessary for the grand transmutation!'

King Krishnadevaraya ordered the treasury to prepare the gold.
Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, before we surrender five thousand gold coins, let me examine the miraculous iron rod.'

Tenali took the rod. He tapped it with a steel hammer, scratched the surface, and smiled.
Tenali said to the alchemist:
'Master Someshwar, your alchemy is magnificent! But why spend five thousand gold coins on distant herbs?
Since your iron rod already possesses the golden touch, let us perform the Reverse Transmutation Test!'

Tenali walked to the palace blacksmith’s forge, picked up a heavy pair of blacksmith’s shears, and cleanly snapped the iron rod in two!
He held up the cross-section before the King:
The iron rod was hollow!
Inside the hollow core, the alchemist had concealed a solid gold cylinder, capped with a thin layer of black wax!
When the tip was heated in the crucible, the wax melted, exposing the pre-existing gold inside!

Tenali smiled:
'Behold the Philosopher’s Stone! The only transmutation taking place was the transmutation of the King’s gold into the swindler’s pocket!'

The alchemist fell to the floor, trembling in terror, confessing his fraud.
King Krishnadevaraya was furious at the deception: he confiscated the alchemist’s tools, banished him from the empire, and awarded the solid gold cylinder to Tenali Raman.
Tenali bowed, reminding the court that real wealth is forged by honest human hands, not by alchemical parlor tricks.
moral: Greedy charlatans who claim to transmute base metals into gold are undone when held to their own alchemical claims.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 74
summary: A wealthy, arrogant nobleman named Gundappa was notorious in Vijayanagara for insulting his hosts. Whenever he was invited to a wedding o...
full_text:
A wealthy, arrogant nobleman named Gundappa was notorious in Vijayanagara for insulting his hosts. Whenever he was invited to a wedding or family feast, he would taste the delicacies, grimace in disgust, and loudly criticize the cooking:
'The rice is too soft! The sambar lacks asafoetida! The payasam is too watery! No one in this city understands culinary refinement like I do!'
Hosts trembled in dread whenever Gundappa visited.

Tenali Raman decided to cure the pompous critic once and for all.
Tenali sent an ornate invitation to Gundappa:
'Noble Lord Gundappa, I have hired the legendary master chefs of the Chola empire to prepare an exclusive Twelve-Course Imperial Feast in your honor at my home.'

Flattered beyond measure, Gundappa arrived in his finest silks, boasting of his refined palate.
Tenali seated him upon a velvet cushion and served the feast upon a fresh banana leaf.

First course: A steaming, fragrant green vegetable soup.
Gundappa took a large spoonful—and his face immediately contorted in horrific agony!
The soup was intensely, excruciatingly bitter!
Tenali smiled politely: 'That is our Imperial Starter: Crushed Wild Bitter Gourd Soup!'

Second course: Crispy fried fritters.
Gundappa took a bite, hoping for relief—it was sliced raw bitter gourd coated in bitter neem paste!
Third course: A dark curry—pure bitter gourd stewed in bitter fenugreek water!
Fourth course: Rice mixed with bitter gourd juice!
Even the sweet pudding at the end was bitter gourd boiled in bitter melon pulp!

Gundappa dropped his silver spoon, tears streaming from his eyes, his mouth burning with intense bitterness:
'Tenali! Art thou trying to poison me? Every single dish is made of bitter gourd! There is not a grain of salt, sugar, or sweetness in this entire feast!'

Tenali Raman looked at him with innocent, wide eyes:
'Why, noble Lord Gundappa! You have spent twenty years spitting out the sweet feasts of honest families, complaining that everything is sour, watery, or flawed!
I thought that a gentleman whose tongue is filled with so much constant bitterness could only appreciate food that matches the flavor of his own speech!
I had my cooks prepare an entire banquet of bitterness to honor your natural disposition!'

Gundappa sat in stunned silence. The biting truth of Tenali’s culinary satire struck him to the core.
He realized how deeply his rude, ungrateful complaints had hurt innocent hosts for decades.
Gundappa bowed his head in genuine shame:
'Tenali, forgive me. My tongue was indeed bitter, and thou hast served me the mirror of my own words.'

Tenali smiled warmly, ordered the bitter gourd cleared away, and brought out a magnificent, delicious feast of sweet coconut rice, mango pachadi, and creamy payasam.
Gundappa ate with humble gratitude, and never again spoke an insulting word at another man’s table.
moral: Pretentious gourmets who complain endlessly about simple hospitality deserve a taste of unvarnished bitterness.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 75
summary: A chest containing ten thousand silver coins disappeared from the imperial tax registry office in Vijayanagara. The Chief Treasurer suspe...
full_text:
A chest containing ten thousand silver coins disappeared from the imperial tax registry office in Vijayanagara.
The Chief Treasurer suspected that one of his four senior accountants had embezzled the funds, but having no proof, could not identify the culprit.
He appealed to Tenali Raman.

Tenali had the four accountants brought into a darkened chamber in the palace.
In the center of the room stood an ornate bronze mirror covered with a dark velvet cloth.
Tenali announced with solemn gravity:
'Brothers, this is the ancient Celestial Mirror of Truth, blessed by Himalayan hermits.
It has a miraculous power:
Each of you must step into this dark room alone, pull aside the cloth, look directly into the glass, and strike the surface gently with your palm.
If you are innocent, the mirror will remain silent and smooth.
But if you are the thief who stole the silver, the mirror will immediately emit a deafening, thunderous roar that will shake the citadel, and your face will turn permanently black in the glass!'

The four accountants listened with beating hearts.
Before the test began, Tenali had privately coated the bronze surface of the mirror with a thick, odorless layer of sticky black lamp-soot!

One by one, the four accountants entered the dark room alone, completed the test, and emerged into the bright audience hall.

Tenali called the four men forward:
'Now, hold up both your palms before His Majesty!'

The first three accountants, whose consciences were completely clear, held up their palms:
Both their palms were coated in thick, black lamp-soot, because they had fearlessly touched the mirror without hesitation!

Then the fourth accountant, a man named Narahari, held up his hands:
His palms were completely, spotlessly clean and white!

Tenali grasped Narahari’s wrist and shouted:
'Behold the thief!'

Narahari trembled in shock: 'What? My hands are clean! How can I be the thief?'

Tenali explained with brilliant psychological logic:
'Thy hands are clean because thy conscience was guilty!
Thou wert so terrified that the mirror would roar and turn thy face black that thou didst not dare touch the glass at all!
The three innocent men touched the mirror without fear, knowing their innocence, and received the soot.
Thou alone didst keep thy hands in thy pockets!'

Narahari broke down in tears, confessed his embezzlement, and revealed where the ten thousand silver coins were hidden beneath his stable floor.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s psychological mastery, proving that an innocent heart fears no test, while guilt betrays itself by its own cowardice.
moral: Guilt makes cowards of us all; those who fear the reflection of truth expose their own dishonesty.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 76
summary: During a freezing winter in Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya announced a royal challenge from his palace balcony: 'If any poor man can ...
full_text:
During a freezing winter in Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya announced a royal challenge from his palace balcony:
'If any poor man can stand chest-deep in the icy cold waters of the palace lake from sunset until dawn, he shall receive a reward of five hundred gold coins and a fertile estate!'

A destitute young weaver named Deva, desperate to buy medicine for his ailing mother and food for his hungry children, accepted the perilous wager.
All through the freezing winter night, with northern winds howling across the lake, Deva stood shivering in the dark, icy water. Whenever his teeth chattered and his limbs grew numb, he fixed his eyes upon a solitary oil lamp glowing gently in a high window of the royal palace two miles away, drawing mental strength from the distant speck of light.
At sunrise, Deva emerged from the lake, blue with cold but alive and victorious!

Deva knelt before King Krishnadevaraya to claim his reward.
The King was about to hand over the gold when an envious courtier whispered:
'Maharaj! The weaver cheated! He confessed that he watched the warm glow of the palace lamp all night! He was warmed by the royal fire!'

King Krishnadevaraya, swayed by the courtier's sophistry, declared:
'Thou hast violated the wager! Thou wert warmed by the heat of the palace lamp! Thou shalt receive no gold!'
Deva was driven out of the palace, weeping in utter despair.

Tenali Raman heard of this cruel injustice.
The next morning, the King invited Tenali to a morning council, but Tenali did not arrive.
Hours passed; noon came, and still Tenali was absent.
Curious, the King rode to Tenali’s house with his courtiers.

In the backyard, the King found Tenali sitting under an ancient banyan tree.
On the ground, Tenali had kindled a tiny fire of dry twigs.
Tied to the highest branch of the banyan tree—forty feet up in the air—hung a small clay cooking pot containing water and rice!

The King stared in disbelief:
'Tenali! What madness is this? Thou hast placed a fire on the grass and hung thy rice pot forty feet up in a tree! How can the rice ever cook?'

Tenali looked up with innocent sincerity:
'Why not, Your Majesty?
If a poor weaver standing two miles away in an icy lake can be thoroughly warmed by the faint light of an oil lamp in a distant palace window, surely my rice pot forty feet above this fire will be cooked in an instant!'

King Krishnadevaraya stood frozen. The biting truth of Tenali’s demonstration struck his heart with overwhelming force.
The King felt deep remorse for his thoughtless cruelty.
He immediately summoned Deva, handed him one thousand gold coins—double the promised reward—along with royal robes of honor, and dismissed the envious courtier from court.
The people cheered Tenali Raman, who used an impossible cooking pot to deliver justice to the poor.
moral: Unreasonable royal judgments that deny rightful rewards must be mirrored by equally absurd logic to awaken conscience.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 77
summary: A proud pundit named Vidyasagara arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he had defeated every philosopher from Kashmir to Ka...
full_text:
A proud pundit named Vidyasagara arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he had defeated every philosopher from Kashmir to Kanyakumari. He planted a red flag in the palace courtyard and issued a challenge:
'Let any scholar of this court debate me on the ultimate metaphysical principle of the cosmos! If none dare face me before sunset, your Emperor must surrender the royal intellectual seal!'

The court scholars sat trembling, knowing Vidyasagara's fierce dialectical reputation.
King Krishnadevaraya looked anxiously at Tenali Raman.

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, I shall debate him right now.'
Tenali stepped onto the debate platform, carrying a small bundle wrapped in fine gold-embroidered silk, resting upon a silver tray.
Tenali placed the bundle upon his desk, closed his eyes, and bowed with theatrical reverence.

Vidyasagara eyed the bundle with deep suspicion:
'What profound scripture hast thou brought to the debate, Tenali?'
Tenali announced with booming authority:
'This, learned pundit, is the supreme southern treatise: *Trinabhimani Samhitasya Tritiya Pariccheda*—The Sacred Doctrine of the Living Blade!
Before we argue, translate for His Majesty the cosmic essence of this work!'

Vidyasagara searched his memory in frantic panic. *Trinabhimani?*
He knew every Upanishad, every sutra, but had never heard of this text!
Fearing that admitting ignorance would shatter his undefeated reputation before the Emperor, Vidyasagara’s knees began to shake.
He stammered, wiped cold sweat from his forehead, and whispered:
'I... I have neglected this specific southern commentary. I yield the debate to Tenali Raman!'
Vidyasagara packed his red flag and fled the court in utter humiliation!

When the challenger had gone, King Krishnadevaraya asked in wonder:
'Tenali! What divine philosophical scripture was inside that silk wrapper?'

Tenali laughed heartily, untied the silk, and dumped the contents onto the table:
Inside was a handful of common green buffalo grass (*Trina*), plucked from the garden lawn!

'Maharaj,' chuckled Tenali, '*Trina* is simply lawn grass!
The proud pundit was so puffed up with big words and complex jargon that a handful of grass wrapped in silk was enough to terrify him into surrender!'

The King and the entire court roared with laughter, celebrating that true wit needs no inflated titles to triumph.
moral: Arrogant intellectuals who brandish long Sanskrit titles are humbled by ordinary grass.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 78
summary: While inspecting the royal gardens, King Krishnadevaraya dropped his heavy gold signet ring down an ancient, narrow stone well. The well ...
full_text:
While inspecting the royal gardens, King Krishnadevaraya dropped his heavy gold signet ring down an ancient, narrow stone well. The well was fifty cubits deep, narrow as an arm, and the bottom was filled with jagged rocks and cold water.
The royal divers shook their heads:
'Maharaj, the shaft is too narrow for any man or boy to descend without suffocating, and long iron hooks cannot locate a tiny ring among the jagged rocks.'

The King turned to Tenali: 'Tenali, canst thou recover my ring without breaking the well stone or sending a man down?'

Tenali replied: 'Easily, Your Majesty! Grant me two hours, a coil of string, and a small copper bowl.'

Tenali procured a small, flat brass bowl and punched a tiny hole in its base.
He then took an enormous round bronze mirror, mounted on a wooden frame, and placed it at the top of the well at an angle that captured the midday sun, directing a concentrated beam of brilliant sunlight straight down the dark, fifty-foot shaft!
The dark depths of the well were instantly illuminated with crystal clarity!
At the bottom, resting upon a flat white river rock, the King's gold signet ring sparkled in the reflected beam of sunlight!

Tenali then smeared the bottom of the brass bowl with a thick, sticky layer of tree-resin and natural pitch (*dammar*).
He tied four strong silk cords to the rim of the bowl and lowered it carefully down the illuminated shaft using the reflected sunbeam as his guide.
Looking down the sunlit well, Tenali maneuvered the cords until the sticky bottom of the bowl rested directly upon the gold ring!

Tenali waited three minutes for the pitch to bond with the metal.
Then he gently pulled the cords upward:
Up came the brass bowl, with the King’s heavy gold signet ring firmly glued to the pitch!

Tenali cleaned the resin with warm oil and handed the sparkling ring to the King!

King Krishnadevaraya and his engineers were awestruck by Tenali’s brilliant synthesis of optics and mechanics:
'Tenali, while my divers thought of swimming, thou didst use the sun as a lantern and tree pitch as a hand!'
The King rewarded Tenali with a purse of gold coins, proving that scientific observation outshines brute force.
moral: Resourceful reflection solves puzzles where dangerous diving only stirs up mud.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 79
summary: A master goldsmith from Tanjore presented King Krishnadevaraya with two magnificent statues of celestial maidens, each three feet high, c...
full_text:
A master goldsmith from Tanjore presented King Krishnadevaraya with two magnificent statues of celestial maidens, each three feet high, cast in solid gold. Both statues had the same weight, the same exquisite smile, and identical craftsmanship.
The goldsmith announced:
'Your Majesty, one statue is worth five thousand gold coins, but the other statue is worth fifty thousand gold coins!
Whosoever can explain the difference without cutting the gold shall receive my master's blessing!'

The court goldsmiths scratched their heads; the scales showed identical weight, and the metal was pure gold in both.
The King turned to Tenali Raman.

Tenali asked for a long, thin, flexible strand of golden wire.
He approached the first statue and found a small hole in its right ear.
He pushed the wire into the ear: the wire traveled through the head and came out through the statue’s open mouth!

Tenali explained:
'Maharaj, this statue represents the untrustworthy gossip.
Whatever secret is confided into his ear immediately spills out through his mouth to cause misery, broken families, and political chaos.
Gold spent on a gossip brings only trouble; this statue is worth the lesser sum.'

Tenali then took the wire and inserted it into the ear of the second statue.
The wire entered, curved downwards into the statue's hollow chest, and remained securely within its golden heart, never emerging from mouth or ear!

Tenali bowed with deep reverence:
'This second statue, Maharaj, represents the true friend, the honorable minister, and the faithful guardian.
Whatever secret, sorrow, or confession is entrusted to his ear is locked forever in the quiet sanctuary of his heart.
He guards confidences with his life, speaks only to heal, and remains steadfast through all trials.
A loyal friend is worth more than fifty thousand gold coins—he is beyond all earthly price!'

The goldsmith bowed low in tears of admiration:
'Tenali Raman, thou hast understood the soul of my art!'
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali, placing the second golden statue in the royal council chamber as an eternal reminder of ministerial integrity.
moral: External appearances cannot reveal virtue; true character is shown by how one receives and handles confidences.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 80
summary: A wealthy, absent-minded merchant named Narahari was taking a sacred bath in the Tungabhadra River before sunrise. Having a valuable gold...
full_text:
A wealthy, absent-minded merchant named Narahari was taking a sacred bath in the Tungabhadra River before sunrise. Having a valuable gold ring set with a large sapphire, he was afraid it might slip off in the deep water.
He walked onto the wide, sandy riverbank, dug a small hole, placed his sapphire ring inside, and covered it with sand.
To remember the spot, he looked up at the sky and saw a fluffy, white morning cloud shaped like a sleeping elephant directly above the hole!
'Excellent!' thought Narahari. 'My ring is buried directly beneath the sleeping elephant cloud!'

After bathing for an hour, Narahari returned to the sand to retrieve his ring.
He looked up: the wind had blown the clouds across the sky!
The sleeping elephant cloud was now three miles away, hovering over the dense forest!
Narahari ran frantically across the forest, digging under every tree, crying that someone had stolen his cloud and his ring!

The weeping merchant came to Tenali Raman.
Tenali listened to his absurd story, chuckled, and said:
'Narahari, he who ties his memory to drifting clouds will spend his life digging in the wind!
Come, let us find thy ring.'

Tenali did not look at the sky.
He asked Narahari: 'When thou didst bury the ring, what did thy feet feel under the sand?'
Narahari remembered: 'My left heel stepped on a large, flat, cold stone slab near the water's edge.'
'And which way was thy shadow falling?'
'The sun was just rising behind the eastern temple spire; my shadow fell straight toward the river.'

Tenali walked to the riverbank, located the flat stone slab, calculated the angle of the sunrise shadow from the temple spire, and marked a circle in the sand thirty paces from the water.
Tenali took a wooden spade, dug two feet into the sand—and out came the sapphire gold ring!

Narahari wept with joy, embracing Tenali:
'Tenali, thou hast recovered my fortune!'
Tenali smiled warmly:
'Remember, Narahari: clouds change their shape and blow away with every breeze, but the temple spire and the stone slab stand firm.
Never anchor thy trust, thy promises, or thy treasures to shifting illusions; anchor them to steadfast truth.'
moral: Fixing reference marks upon shifting, moving objects guarantees failure; anchor thy memory to the eternal.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 81
summary: A gigantic warrior and martial artist named Malakallu arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, wearing heavy armor and carrying an enormous ...
full_text:
A gigantic warrior and martial artist named Malakallu arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, wearing heavy armor and carrying an enormous iron club. He had defeated dozens of champions in wrestling and swordplay.
Malakallu slammed a pair of thick iron sandals onto the King’s audience carpet, boasting:
'I challenge the scholars and ministers of Vijayanagara to a duel of endurance!
Whosoever can wear these solid iron sandals, walk across fifty paces of glowing charcoal, and emerge without injury shall be crowned Champion of the Deccan!
If none dare, your Emperor must acknowledge that your courtiers are cowards!'

The court was silent in dismay. Walking across burning charcoal in solid iron sandals would roast a man’s feet to the bone, as iron conducts intense heat instantly!
King Krishnadevaraya looked anxiously at Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward with a serene smile:
'I accept the challenge, Malakallu! But according to ancient codes of honor, since thou didst choose the sandals, I have the right to set the testing conditions!'
Malakallu laughed arrogance: 'Set whatever conditions thou wilt, jester!'

Tenali said: 'Very well! We shall both wear iron sandals and walk across the coals.
However, ancient codes state that champions must face the trial simultaneously, side by side!
Furthermore, to ensure absolute fairness, thy iron sandals shall be tied to thy feet with ropes of pitch-soaked hemp, and my sandals shall be tied to mine!'

Malakallu agreed, boasting: 'I fear nothing!'

The charcoal pit was prepared in the palace courtyard, glowing red-hot with intense heat.
Tenali had the royal blacksmiths strap the heavy iron sandals securely to Malakallu’s feet with pitch-soaked ropes.
Tenali then put on his own pair of iron sandals.

As they stood at the edge of the blazing pit, Tenali turned to the King and proclaimed:
'Maharaj, let the duel begin!
According to the rules of simultaneous trial, the challenger must step onto the coals first to lead the way, and I shall step immediately behind him!'

Malakallu looked at the glowing coals, then looked at his heavy iron sandals strapped to his feet.
He suddenly realized the horrific reality:
The moment his iron sandals touched the glowing coals, the iron would superheat within seconds, the pitch-soaked ropes would catch fire, and his feet would be incinerated before he could take three steps!
He would be roasted alive!

Malakallu’s courage evaporated into sheer panic.
He backed away frantically, screaming:
'No! I yield! Unstrap these sandals! I withdraw the challenge!'

He fell to the floor, sweating and trembling, begging for royal pardon!
The entire court burst into roaring laughter as the boastful giant squirmed to unstrap his own iron shoes!

Tenali smiled, took off his unheated sandals, and said:
'True valor does not consist in creating cruel, destructive trials to humiliate others. A man who lives by the fire of arrogance is always the first to be burned by his own flames!'

The King banished the bully, rewarding Tenali Raman for defending the honor of Vijayanagara without spilling a single drop of blood.
moral: Boastful champions who threaten peaceful courts with violent wagers are disarmed by quick-witted rules of engagement.
