title: Tenali Raman Tale 82
summary: Two neighboring farmers, Venkanna and Ramanna, appeared before King Krishnadevaraya claiming ownership of an ancient, prize mango tree th...
full_text:
Two neighboring farmers, Venkanna and Ramanna, appeared before King Krishnadevaraya claiming ownership of an ancient, prize mango tree that grew precisely upon the earthen boundary ridge dividing their lands.
The tree yielded thousands of sweet Alphonso mangoes every summer.
Venkanna swore: 'My grandfather planted the seed fifty years ago! It belongs entirely to me!'
Ramanna shouted: 'A lie! My father watered it and pruned its branches; it is mine!'

Both men produced contradictory land records, and the village elders were divided into two warring factions.
The King was exhausted: 'If neither will compromise, I shall order the royal woodcutters to saw the tree in half down the middle, so each farmer receives half the timber!'

Venkanna eagerly nodded:
'Yes, Maharaj! A wise verdict! Cut the tree in half! If I cannot have the whole tree, let Ramanna get only half of a dead trunk!'

Ramanna, hearing the decree, threw himself at the King’s feet, weeping bitterly:
'No, Maharaj! I beg of you, do not destroy the tree!
That tree has provided shade to our children and sweet fruit to our families for two generations!
Give the entire tree to Venkanna! Let it live and bear fruit, even if I receive not a single mango!'

King Krishnadevaraya was about to finalize the award when Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, the true owner of the tree has just revealed himself!'

Tenali pointed to Ramanna:
'Look at the two men!
Venkanna was willing to see the living tree destroyed and turned to firewood, because he cares only for selfish spite!
Ramanna was willing to sacrifice his own harvest and give up the tree, because his heart loves the living tree and cannot bear to see it slain!
Only the man who nurtured the tree with love cares for its life!'

King Krishnadevaraya recognized the profound Solomon-like wisdom of Tenali’s deduction.
The King awarded the entire mango tree and the boundary ridge to Ramanna.
Venkanna was fined fifty silver coins for perjury and ordered to plant ten new mango saplings along the public road.
The people praised Tenali’s deep understanding that true love always chooses preservation over destruction.
moral: A parent’s true love protects the welfare of the child, while selfish greed cares only for the prize.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 83
summary: King Krishnadevaraya gave fifty tolas of pure, refined gold bullion from the royal treasury to the chief court goldsmith, Master Subbiah,...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya gave fifty tolas of pure, refined gold bullion from the royal treasury to the chief court goldsmith, Master Subbiah, commanding him to craft a magnificent ceremonial golden crown adorned with pearls for the coronation festival.
When Subbiah delivered the finished crown, it was a masterpiece of filigree and design, and when placed upon the scale, it weighed precisely fifty tolas.

However, a rumor reached the King that Subbiah had secretly kept ten tolas of pure gold for himself, substituting an equal weight of cheap copper and silver inside the molten alloy!
The King was troubled:
'How can we prove whether the gold is pure without melting the crown and destroying this exquisite work of art?'

The royal scholars were baffled.
Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, the great Greek sage Archimedes discovered that every metal displaces a specific volume of water according to its natural density. Let us perform the Water Displacement Trial.'

Tenali procured a large, cylindrical brass vessel filled to the absolute brim with water, resting inside a dry, shallow silver basin.
Tenali took fifty tolas of pure, unadulterated gold bullion from the treasury and lowered it gently into the water.
A certain amount of water overflowed into the silver basin.
Tenali measured the overflow water with a marked glass cylinder:
It measured precisely **five measures** of water.

Tenali then emptied the basin, refilled the brass vessel to the brim, and lowered the finished golden crown into the water!
If the crown were pure gold, it should displace precisely five measures of water.
However, because copper and silver are less dense than gold, a crown containing ten tolas of copper and silver occupies greater volume!
The crown caused **seven measures** of water to overflow into the silver basin!

Tenali smiled and presented the measured water to the King:
'Maharaj, the scales of weight can be deceived by mixing metals, but the scales of water cannot be lied to!
The crown displaced two extra measures of water, proving beyond all doubt that cheaper, lighter metals were mixed into the alloy to inflate its volume!'

Faced with undeniable scientific proof, the goldsmith collapsed in terror, confessed that he had stolen ten tolas of gold, and surrendered the hidden bullion.
The King rewarded Tenali with a gold chain, marveling at how practical science and sharp observation protect justice in the imperial court.
moral: Deceitful adulteration of honest wealth is exposed by nature's immutable laws of density and displacement.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 84
summary: An arrogant courtier named Somadeva was desperate to impress King Krishnadevaraya with his supposed 'esoteric intuition'. Whenever the Ki...
full_text:
An arrogant courtier named Somadeva was desperate to impress King Krishnadevaraya with his supposed 'esoteric intuition'. Whenever the King spoke of military maneuvers, Somadeva would nod knowingly and whisper:
'Yes, Maharaj! I sensed that through my mystical intuition! I can hear what common ears cannot!'

Tenali Raman decided to cure the courtier of his pretentious clairvoyance.

King Krishnadevaraya had recently purchased an old cavalry horse that had gone completely, stone-deaf due to cannon fire in an ancient border siege.
Tenali brought the deaf horse to the palace courtyard where Somadeva was boasting to other courtiers.

Tenali whispered to Somadeva with an air of urgent mystery:
'Friend Somadeva, this is no ordinary cavalry horse. It is a sacred "Oracle Steed" from the Himalayas!
When you hold your ear close to its mouth, it whispers secret prophecies about the future of the empire!
I listened just now, and it spoke of great glory. But only a man of profound esoteric intuition like you can understand its deeper cosmic messages!'

Somadeva’s vanity was instantly ignited:
'Of course, Tenali! My ears are attuned to the cosmic frequencies!'

Somadeva walked up to the old horse, bowed with great ceremony, and leaned his right ear directly against the horse’s lips.
The horse, which was stone-deaf and had no idea what was happening, simply chewed its oats contentedly.

After three minutes of theatrical listening, Somadeva stood up, his face filled with profound, spiritual awe:
'Ah! Transcendent wisdom! The sacred steed spoke to me in ancient celestial Sanskrit!
It whispered: "The Emperor’s fame shall conquer the three worlds, and Somadeva shall be appointed Chief Counselor of State!"'

Tenali Raman burst into body-shaking, roaring laughter!
King Krishnadevaraya and the courtiers, who had been watching from the balcony, broke into deafening applause and laughter!

The King came down the stairs, laughing so hard he wiped tears from his eyes:
'Somadeva! Thou hast heard celestial Sanskrit from a horse that has been completely, stone-deaf for eight years!'

Tenali clapped the courtier on the shoulder:
'A deaf horse speaks nothing, but a vain fool hears whatever flattery pleases his pride!'

Somadeva turned bright purple, shrank with humiliation, and fled the courtyard.
He never again claimed to possess 'esoteric intuition', while Tenali showed that pretentious vanity makes a man hear voices in empty air.
moral: Pretending to hear secrets to appear wise leads to comedic humiliation; honest listening is the foundation of truth.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 85
summary: An elderly blind beggar named Suradas sat daily outside the temple gates of Vijayanagara, singing devotional hymns. Over twenty years of ...
full_text:
An elderly blind beggar named Suradas sat daily outside the temple gates of Vijayanagara, singing devotional hymns. Over twenty years of frugal living, he had saved forty silver coins in a small leather pouch, which he kept tied securely around his waist to buy food in his old age.

One afternoon, while Suradas was praying, a greedy butcher named Kasim noticed the pouch, sliced the cord with his meat knife, and snatched the purse!
Suradas cried out, grabbing Kasim’s coat.
The butcher shouted: 'Liar! This is my purse! I earned these forty silver coins selling mutton in my shop today!'
Because the beggar was blind and had no witnesses, the temple guards brought both men before Tenali Raman.

Kasim swore: 'The money is mine! Why should a blind beggar have forty silver coins?'
Suradas wept: 'I saved them coin by coin for twenty years, master!'

Tenali looked at the leather purse.
He called for a large, shallow bowl of pure, boiling hot water.
Tenali untied the purse and emptied the forty silver coins straight into the steaming hot water!

Tenali, the King, and the assembly watched the surface of the water intently.
If the coins had belonged to a butcher who handled meat and animal fat all day, greasy oil droplets and fat residues would immediately rise to the surface of the hot water, forming a slick film.
However, the surface of the water remained crystal clear! Not a single droplet of grease appeared!

Instead, a faint, sweet, unmistakable fragrance of temple incense, crushed jasmine petals, and camphor rose with the steam from the hot water!
The coins had been stored for years in the beggar’s cloth beside the temple incense burners!

Tenali smiled and pointed to the clear, fragrant water:
'The coins have given their testimony!
Money from a butcher shop carries the grease of animal fat; money saved outside a temple carries the fragrance of incense and flowers!
These coins never saw a butcher's stall!'

Faced with this undeniable forensic proof, the butcher confessed his crime.
The King ordered the butcher fined eighty silver coins—which were given to Suradas—and sentenced the thief to three months of community labor.
Suradas wept tears of gratitude, praising Tenali Raman as the living eyes of justice for the blind.
moral: Forensic examination of coins reveals their recent history; truth defends the defenseless against ruthless theft.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 86
summary: In a whimsical and eccentric mood, King Krishnadevaraya decided to challenge the court with an impossible command: 'Within three days, my...
full_text:
In a whimsical and eccentric mood, King Krishnadevaraya decided to challenge the court with an impossible command:
'Within three days, my royal dairy must present me with a silver cup filled with pure, fresh milk milked from a sturdy male bullock!
If my ministers cannot provide bull's milk, each shall be fined five hundred gold coins!'

The ministers went home in utter despair. Male bullocks do not produce milk; it is a biological impossibility!
'The King has lost his reason,' moaned the Prime Minister. 'We must pay the fine!'

Tenali Raman smiled: 'Do not pay a single copper. I shall provide the King with his bull's milk.'

On the morning of the third day, the court assembled.
All the ministers sat trembling, unable to produce the milk.
Tenali Raman entered the hall, dressed in disheveled robes, his hair uncombed, looking utterly exhausted, panting and groaning as he walked.

King Krishnadevaraya frowned:
'Tenali! What has happened to thee? Why art thou so exhausted and untidy?'

Tenali bowed with an expression of immense, weary relief:
'Jahanpanah! Pardon my condition! I have spent the entire night acting as a midwife, assisting my elderly uncle who was in terrible labor, helping him give birth to a bouncing baby boy!'

The King stared at Tenali in stunned bewilderment:
'Tenali, art thou completely mad? A man giving birth to a baby?
Men do not give birth! It is an absolute, natural impossibility!'

Tenali Raman looked up with radiant, sparkling wit:
'Precisely, Your Majesty!
If a man cannot give birth to a baby because of the immutable laws of nature, how can a male bullock give milk?
Nature gave milk only to the mother cow, just as nature gave childbearing only to women!
When an Emperor commands his ministers to milk a bull, he asks nature to violate its own sacred laws!'

King Krishnadevaraya sat back on his throne, stunned for a moment, and then burst into hearty, roaring laughter!
'Ha-ha-ha! Tenali, thou hast caught me in my own trap of folly!'
The King canceled the absurd fine, rewarded Tenali with a gold medal, and praised his courage in holding up the mirror of reason to royal whims.
moral: An absurd demand can only be answered by demonstrating an equally absurd biological impossibility.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 87
summary: A flamboyant palmist and astrologer named Jyotishi Shankara set up an ornate canopy in the main bazaar of Vijayanagara, wearing an enormo...
full_text:
A flamboyant palmist and astrologer named Jyotishi Shankara set up an ornate canopy in the main bazaar of Vijayanagara, wearing an enormous turban of gold-threaded silk adorned with peacock feathers.
He proclaimed to the crowds:
'I read the lines of destiny with absolute infallibility! I foresee all events that will occur to any man ten years into the future!'
Citizens paid silver coins to hear flattering prophecies of wealth and marriage.

Tenali Raman walked past the booth, observing the charlatan fleece poor laborers.
Tenali decided to demonstrate the fraud before the entire bazaar.

Tenali stood in the crowd, watching the astrologer hold a customer’s palm.
Tenali quietly untied his light bamboo walking staff.
With a swift, deft, upward flick of his staff, Tenali hooked the brim of the astrologer's magnificent golden turban, flicked it off the man’s head, and sent it flying straight into an open basket of fresh, sticky black dates at the neighboring fruit stall!

The turban landed upside down with a wet squelch, completely smothered in black date syrup and squashed fruit!

The astrologer leaped up, bareheaded and bald, shrieking in furious outrage:
'Insolent villain! Who knocked off my golden turban? Who ruined my expensive silk hat?'

Tenali Raman stepped forward, smiling with delightful innocence:
'Why, great Astrologer! You claimed to foresee the fate of every stranger ten years into the future!
How is it that with all your celestial vision, you could not foresee that your own turban would fly into a basket of sticky dates five seconds ago?
If your stars cannot warn you about your own hat, how dare you charge silver to predict the life of another man?'

The entire marketplace erupted in roaring laughter!
The customers demanded their silver back, laughing at the bald astrologer struggling to scrape date syrup from his ruined turban.
The charlatan packed his charts and fled Vijayanagara, while Tenali showed that practical proof easily dismantles false claims of omniscience.
moral: Those who claim to foresee the distant future of strangers cannot even foresee the loss of their own hats.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 88
summary: Envious courtiers who wanted to eliminate Tenali Raman convinced King Krishnadevaraya that royal health required an extraordinary medicin...
full_text:
Envious courtiers who wanted to eliminate Tenali Raman convinced King Krishnadevaraya that royal health required an extraordinary medicine:
'Maharaj, your royal vitality requires the most potent tonic known to Ayurveda: pure, fresh milk from a wild tigress nursing her cubs in the jungle!
Only a man of supreme courage and resourcefulness can fetch it—and none is more capable than Tenali Raman!'

The King, in a whimsical mood, commanded Tenali:
'Tenali, venture into the Dandaka forest and bring me a cup of fresh tigress's milk within seven days, or face royal displeasure!'

The courtiers smirked, expecting Tenali to be torn to pieces by tigers or banished for failure.
Tenali bowed: 'Your command shall be fulfilled, Maharaj.'

Tenali did not walk into the tiger’s lair to be eaten.
He went to the village of a pastoral shepherd community and found a magnificent, large wild mountain goat whose milk was unusually thick and creamy.
Tenali paid the shepherd for a brass pot of the rich goat's milk.

Tenali then spent five days walking through thorny mountain brush, deliberately tearing his silk coat, scratching his arms and face with harmless brambles, and rubbing red clay onto his trousers.

On the seventh day, Tenali staggered into King Krishnadevaraya’s audience hall.
He looked battered, bleeding from minor scratches, his clothes in rags, panting as though he had wrestled ten demons!
In his trembling hand, he held a sealed golden goblet covered with a tiger skin!

The King sprang from his throne in alarm:
'Tenali! What happened to thee? Thou art wounded!'

Tenali gasped with theatrical heroism:
'Jahanpanah! I fought through the deepest caves of the Dandaka jungle!
I located a fierce, ten-foot man-eating tigress nursing four cubs!
I wrestled the beast for three hours, pinned her claws to the cave wall, and milked this cup from her breast with my own hands!
Here is your tigress’s milk, Maharaj!'

The King stared at the goblet, then at the blood and torn clothes on Tenali:
'Tenali, this is miraculous valor!'

Tenali smiled and said:
'However, Maharaj, the royal physicians who prescribed this medicine must administer it!
Our ancient Ayurvedic texts state that whoever drinks tigress's milk must also be massaged with the tigress’s claws, and the courtiers who suggested this cure must accompany me back to the jungle to return the tigress her cup!'

The envious courtiers turned green with absolute terror, falling to their knees, begging the King:
'No, no, Your Majesty! The cure is too dangerous! We withdraw the recommendation!'

The King laughed, realizing the brilliant comedy of Tenali’s adventure.
He rewarded Tenali with five hundred gold coins for his 'heroic scratches', while the schemers learned never to set traps for the master of wit.
moral: When power demands impossible and perilous tasks, wit provides a safe and humorous escape.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 89
summary: A wealthy, tyrannical landlord named Somappa made a cruel bet with a poor tenant farmer named Somu, who owed thirty bags of grain: 'If th...
full_text:
A wealthy, tyrannical landlord named Somappa made a cruel bet with a poor tenant farmer named Somu, who owed thirty bags of grain:
'If thou canst stand in the frozen temple tank up to thy waist for the entire night from dusk to dawn without warm clothes, thy debt shall be forgiven! If thou failest, I shall seize thy children as bonded servants!'

Desperate to protect his family, Somu stood in the freezing water all night, his limbs turning blue, his teeth chattering in agony.
At dawn, Somu crawled out alive and demanded the debt receipt.
The cruel landlord refused, sneering:
'Thou didst look at the burning cremation fire on the distant hill! Thou wert warmed by the smoke! Thy debt stands!'

Somu came weeping to Tenali Raman.
Tenali’s heart burned with righteous fury at the landlord’s cruelty.

Tenali invited Landlord Somappa to a grand banquet at his house that evening.
Somappa arrived, expecting rich dishes.
Instead, Tenali led Somappa into his garden, where an open stone pool was filled with ice-cold mountain water.
Tenali’s burly servants seized the landlord, stripped him of his velvet coat, and placed him in the freezing water!

Somappa shrieked, shivering and weeping:
'Tenali! What madness is this? I am freezing to death! Release me!'

Tenali sat fifty yards away on a terrace beside a roaring charcoal fire, roasting succulent sweet potatoes and sipping hot spiced tea.
Tenali called out cheerfully:
'Why dost thou complain, friend Somappa? Look at my roaring charcoal fire fifty yards away!
According to thy own legal theory, the heat from my fire is blowing across the grass and thoroughly warming thee in the water!
Stay in the tank until sunrise, and thou shalt be as warm as a roast pheasant!'

Somappa’s teeth chattered violently, his lips turned blue, and he screamed in agonizing repentance:
'Mercy, Tenali! I was a monster! I lied! Fire fifty yards away cannot warm a man freezing in icy water!
Release me! I forgive Somu’s debt forever, and I will give him the land deed as a gift!'

Tenali had the legal debt release and land deed signed on the spot by Somappa’s trembling hands before pulling him from the pool.
Tenali wrapped the shivering landlord in a blanket, fed him hot ginger tea, and said:
'Never impose a cruelty upon another man that thine own soft flesh cannot endure for ten minutes.'

Somu received his freedom and his land, while Somappa became a humble, generous man, cured of his tyranny forever.
moral: Cruelty cloaked in impossible wagers is defeated when the tyrant is forced to feel the cold truth.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 90
summary: A vain and wealthy textile merchant named Shreshthi Manikchand was obsessed with appearances. He wore fine silks, perfumed his mustache w...
full_text:
A vain and wealthy textile merchant named Shreshthi Manikchand was obsessed with appearances. He wore fine silks, perfumed his mustache with musk, and bragged that everything he owned was of pure gold or celestial quality.
One afternoon, during a public gathering at the town square, Manikchand pointed to a passing washerman’s grey donkey and sneered:
'Look at that wretched beast! Common folk surround themselves with coarse, ugly animals. If I owned a donkey, I would wash its tail with rosewater and imported silk soap every morning until the hair turned into pure, shining golden silk!'

The crowd laughed at his arrogant boasting.
Tenali Raman, who was standing nearby, resolved to test the merchant's claim.

The next morning, Tenali arrived outside Manikchand’s grand mansion leading an old, patient grey donkey.
Tenali tied the donkey to the merchant's front gatepost, pulled up a wooden stool, brought out a copper bowl of warm water, a bar of soap, and began scrubbing the donkey's coarse tail with immense, theatrical concentration!

A large crowd gathered to watch.
Tenali lathered the donkey’s tail with soap, rinsed it, combed the coarse hairs, and repeated the process:
Lather, rinse, scrub, comb!
The donkey occasionally swished its wet tail, splattering soapy water across Tenali’s face and clothes!

Merchant Manikchand stepped out of his mansion, frowning in annoyance:
'Tenali! Why art thou washing that dirty donkey’s tail at my front gate, blocking my customers?'

Tenali looked up with earnest sincerity:
'Shreshthi-ji! I am putting your brilliant doctrine into practice!
You proclaimed yesterday that by washing a donkey's tail with soap and devotion, the coarse hair would turn into pure, shining golden silk!
I have been scrubbing for three hours, and I am waiting for the gold to appear!'

Manikchand stammered, his face reddening:
'Tenali, art thou a fool? No matter how much soap thou usest, a donkey’s tail is made of coarse hair; it will never turn into silk!'

Tenali stood up, wiped the soap foam from his eyes, and addressed the laughing crowd:
'Hear the wise merchant’s confession!
A donkey’s tail remains a donkey’s tail, no matter how much rosewater and soap thou washest it with!
And an arrogant man remains a hollow boaster, no matter how many fine silk robes he wears to disguise his empty mind!'

The entire crowd roared with laughter, clapping and cheering.
Manikchand retreated into his mansion in utter disgrace, cured of his boastful vanity, while Tenali untied the donkey and returned it to the washerman with a basket of fresh greens.
moral: Pretentious vanity that seeks to transform basic reality into false luxury makes itself an object of ridicule.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 91
summary: A wealthy and merciless moneylender named Dhaniram took advantage of an impoverished traveling merchant named Madhava. During a swelterin...
full_text:
A wealthy and merciless moneylender named Dhaniram took advantage of an impoverished traveling merchant named Madhava.
During a sweltering summer noon, Madhava, exhausted and faint from heat, sat down to rest for an hour in the cool shade cast by the wall of Dhaniram’s mansion.
When Madhava stood up to resume his journey, Dhaniram ran out and demanded five silver coins!
'Thou didst use the shade of my private mansion wall to cool thy body!' shouted Dhaniram. 'The shade belongs to my property; pay for the shadow or I will have the guards seize thy baggage!'

The poor merchant was stunned, having no money.
Tenali Raman, who was passing by, witnessed the extortion.
Tenali stepped forward:
'Dhaniram is legally correct! Property rights must be respected! Let us settle this account before King Krishnadevaraya.'

They went to the royal court.
Dhaniram presented his claim: 'Maharaj, the merchant consumed the cool shadow of my wall; he must pay five silver coins!'
The King frowned, disgusted by the usurer’s shameless greed, but struggled to find a legal precedent.

Tenali Raman smiled:
'Maharaj, I shall settle the payment immediately on behalf of the poor traveler.'

Tenali had a large, polished silver tray placed upon the sunny courtyard floor.
Tenali took five bright silver coins from his own purse and arranged them in a row upon the edge of the tray.
The bright midday sun cast the dark, distinct shadows of the five silver coins across the surface of the silver tray!

Tenali pointed to the tray and said:
'Master Dhaniram, step forward and receive your payment!
The traveler used the shadow of your wall to cool himself; he did not remove a single brick, stone, or drop of mortar from your house.
Therefore, it is only just that you take the shadow of these five silver coins to enrich your purse!
Reach out your hands, scoop up the five shadows from the tray, and take them home to your treasury!'

The court erupted in thunderous applause and laughter!
Dhaniram stood humiliated, unable to pick up a shadow.
He stammered: 'I cannot pick up a shadow!'

Tenali replied with ringing moral authority:
'If you cannot pick up a shadow of money, how dare you charge real silver for the shadow of a wall?
Heaven made the sun and the shade for all living creatures. Whosoever charges money for cool air and shade is a thief of nature’s bounty!'

King Krishnadevaraya fined the greedy moneylender fifty silver coins for harassing travelers, and Tenali’s witty justice was celebrated throughout the capital.
moral: Extortionate usurers who demand payment for non-existent services must be repaid with the shadows of money.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 92
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, an enthusiastic patron of the arts, visited the studio of the celebrated royal court painter, Master Raghunath. The...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, an enthusiastic patron of the arts, visited the studio of the celebrated royal court painter, Master Raghunath.
The painter unveiled a magnificent landscape depicting a galloping warhorse:
The front half of the horse—its noble head, flaring nostrils, muscular chest, and powerful front legs—was rendered with breathtaking realism, charging forward, while the rear half was hidden behind a picturesque stone wall and flowering oleander bushes.

All the courtiers praised the painting.
However, King Krishnadevaraya, in a critical mood, frowned and pointed at the canvas:
'Raghunath, where is the other half of the horse?
Where are its hind legs? Where is its tail?
Thou hast painted only half a horse! How can I pay full price for half an animal?'

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, great art does not insult the viewer by spelling out every obvious detail; it speaks to the imagination!
The horse’s rear half is safely behind the wall! A man of refined artistic intellect visualizes the complete steed through the power of his mind!'

The King laughed playfully:
'Tenali, thou art always defending painters.
I give thee one month: paint me a canvas that requires imagination, and if it fails to impress me, thou shalt be fined five hundred gold coins!'

One month later, Tenali Raman arrived at the royal audience hall carrying a large, framed canvas covered with a fine silk cloth.
The King and the courtiers gathered eagerly.
Tenali unveiled the canvas:

The canvas was completely, spotlessly, uniformly white!
Near the bottom edge, there were three tiny strokes of green paint resembling blades of grass, and nothing else!

The King stared, bewildered and annoyed:
'Tenali! What is this? The canvas is empty! What hast thou painted?'

Tenali bowed with supreme dignity:
'Maharaj! This is my masterwork: *The Royal Stallion Grazing on Green Pastures*!'

The King frowned: 'Where is the green pasture?'
Tenali replied: 'The horse ate all the grass, Maharaj! That is why only three tiny blades remain at the bottom!'

The King shouted: 'And where is the horse?'
Tenali smiled with dazzling wit:
'Why, Your Majesty! Having eaten all the grass, do you expect a sensible horse to stand around staring at an empty white canvas?
The horse has already galloped back to the royal stables to drink water!
Apply your royal imagination, Maharaj, and visualize the magnificent steed galloping across the distant hills!'

King Krishnadevaraya was stunned for a moment, then burst into uncontrollable, body-shaking laughter!
'Ha-ha-ha! Tenali, thou hast paid me back for my criticism of Master Raghunath’s painting!'
The King rewarded Tenali with five hundred gold coins, and officially apologized to the court painter, acknowledging that art and imagination must walk hand in hand.
moral: True art invites the imagination to complete the vision; literal-minded criticism reveals only the critic's lack of depth.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 93
summary: A wealthy, vain merchant named Lakshmipati hosted a grand feast for the city councilors of Vijayanagara. To display his immense wealth, h...
full_text:
A wealthy, vain merchant named Lakshmipati hosted a grand feast for the city councilors of Vijayanagara. To display his immense wealth, he served each guest with a spoon cast in solid gold.
Throughout the dinner, Lakshmipati repeatedly reminded his guests:
'Look at the golden spoons! Was there ever such magnificence? Eating with pure gold purifies the soul and elevates the flavor of the food!'

Tenali Raman sat quietly, eating his rice and lentil dal.
As the feast concluded, Tenali picked up his golden spoon, wiped it clean with his linen napkin, and deliberately slipped it into the inner pocket of his coat before the eyes of the host!

Lakshmipati was horrified: 'Tenali! Thou hast stolen my golden spoon! Put it back immediately!'

Tenali looked astonished:
'Stolen? Why, noble Lakshmipati! Didst thou not declare that eating with gold purifies the soul and elevates the food?
My poor digestion has been troubled for years; I thought that keeping this golden spoon near my stomach would cure my liver!'

Lakshmipati grew furious:
'Tenali, stop this ridiculous nonsense! A golden spoon is made of heavy metal; it cannot cure a sick stomach! Its only value is that it costs fifty gold dinars!'

Tenali smiled with penetrating wisdom:
'Aha! Then why didst thou boast for three hours that the spoon possessed magical spiritual virtue?
A golden spoon cannot make sour curry sweet, nor can it make a greedy man noble.
When a hungry beggar eats simple porridge with his fingers with a clean heart, his meal is blessed; but when a vain man eats with a golden spoon while despising the poor, his gold is only heavy dirt.'

Tenali placed the golden spoon back upon the silver platter.
Lakshmipati lowered his eyes in shame, recognizing that true nobility is found in generous hospitality, not in ostentatious cutlery.
moral: True nourishment comes from honest food, not from the golden utensils that carry it.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 94
summary: An ambassador from the court of Isfahan arrived in Vijayanagara, presenting three philosophical riddles to King Krishnadevaraya: 'First: ...
full_text:
An ambassador from the court of Isfahan arrived in Vijayanagara, presenting three philosophical riddles to King Krishnadevaraya:
'First: Where is the exact center of the earth?
Second: How many stars shine in the heavens?
Third: What is the exact difference between a wise man and a fool?'

The court scholars attempted complex mathematical calculations of spheres and constellations, but none could satisfy the foreign envoy.
Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, I shall answer the ambassador’s questions immediately.'

Tenali took an iron peg and a mallet. He walked to the exact center of the palace audience hall, drove the peg firmly into the floor tiles, and announced:
'Here, noble envoy, is the exact center of the earth!
If you doubt my calculation, take your measuring ropes and measure the earth in all four directions. If it is off by even an inch, I will surrender my head!'
The envoy smiled wryly, unable to measure the planet.

For the second question, Tenali brought a fat, woolly mountain ram into the hall.
Tenali pointed to the ram’s dense, curly fleece:
'There are precisely as many stars in the heavens as there are hairs upon the body of this ram!
If you do not believe me, count the hairs on this ram, and then count the stars in the sky. If the counts differ by a single hair, my answer is void!'
The envoy laughed, recognizing the impossible parallel.

For the third question, Tenali asked: 'What is the difference between a wise man and a fool?'
Tenali pointed to the court:
'A wise man knows when he does not know, and remains silent to observe and learn.
A fool pretends to know everything, asking unanswerable questions to trap others, while remaining blind to the truth before his feet!'

The Persian envoy was enchanted by Tenali’s brilliant philosophical agility.
He bowed low, presented Tenali with a chest of Persian carpets and rosewater, declaring that Vijayanagara possessed the sharpest intellect in the Orient.
moral: Cosmic riddles are solved through the profound geometry of human existence.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 95
summary: While walking through an ancient cemetery outside Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya kicked an old human skull that lay in the dry grass....
full_text:
While walking through an ancient cemetery outside Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya kicked an old human skull that lay in the dry grass.
The King sighed:
'Tenali, look upon this skull. It once had eyes that saw, ears that heard, and a tongue that spoke.
I wonder what fatal error brought this man to his early grave?'

Tenali bent down, examined the skull closely, and said with a solemn whisper:
'Maharaj, the skull just whispered its secret to me!'
The King stared: 'What did it say?'
Tenali replied:
'The skull whispered: "My tongue was too long, and my ears were too short; loose speech brought me to this dust!"'

The King scoffed: 'Nonsense! Skulls do not talk!'
Tenali insisted: 'I swear it, Maharaj! Bring the skull to court tomorrow, and it will speak before your throne!'

The next morning, the skull was placed upon a velvet cushion in the royal diwan.
The King commanded: 'Tenali, make the skull speak, or thou shalt be punished for mocking the Emperor!'

Tenali tapped the skull gently with his stylus:
'Speak, skull! Tell the Emperor how thou didst meet thy death!'
The skull remained completely silent.
Tenali asked again: 'Speak, skull!'
Not a whisper emerged.

The King grew furious:
'Tenali, thou hast lied to thy King!
Guards! Take Tenali to the palace gate and strike his back with twenty strokes of the cane for insolence!'

As the guards seized Tenali, Tenali looked back at the silent skull, smiled through his pain, and addressed the King:
'Maharaj! Look at the skull now!
Did it not tell the absolute truth?
Yesterday, it warned: "Loose speech brings a man to grief!"
Because my own tongue spoke too loosely yesterday about talking skulls, I am receiving twenty strokes of the cane today!
The skull did not need to speak with vocal cords; its lesson was delivered upon my own back!'

King Krishnadevaraya stopped in his tracks, realizing the profound, self-sacrificing wit of Tenali’s demonstration.
The King ordered the guards to release Tenali immediately, rewarded him with twenty gold coins instead of cane strokes, and had the lesson inscribed upon the gates:
'Guard thy tongue, for an unruly tongue digs an early grave.'
moral: Loose talk and unguarded tongues bring swift ruin; silence is the fortress of the wise.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 96
summary: An impoverished farmer named Mallesh came weeping to the court of Vijayanagara. His neighbor, a wealthy and aggressive landholder named B...
full_text:
An impoverished farmer named Mallesh came weeping to the court of Vijayanagara.
His neighbor, a wealthy and aggressive landholder named Bhupati, had secretly moved the ancient granite boundary stone dividing their properties twenty yards into Mallesh’s land during a moonless night, stealing three fertile acres of cotton fields!
When Mallesh protested, Bhupati claimed:
'The stone has stood in this exact spot for a hundred years! Look at how deeply it is embedded in the soil!'

The village council was intimidated by Bhupati’s wealth, and the King sent Tenali Raman to investigate.

Tenali inspected the granite boundary stone.
The stone was indeed set deep in the earth, and the surrounding soil had been tamped down with water to look undisturbed.
Tenali smiled calmly: 'Dig up the stone!'

The workers dug a trench around the stone and hauled it out of the ground.
Tenali examined the earth beneath the stone’s base:
The soil was loose, fresh, and underneath lay green, crushed grass that had not yet turned brown!
Grass crushed beneath a stone for a hundred years turns to black ash within three months; green grass proves the stone was placed there within forty-eight hours!

Furthermore, Tenali pointed to an ancient neem tree standing twenty yards away on the ridge:
'Look at the roots of this neem tree!
Tree roots grow away from heavy stone obstacles.
The ancient groove where the boundary stone rested for fifty years is visible twenty yards back, where the neem roots formed a deep hollow!'

Tenali ordered workers to dig at the old groove:
There, beneath the soil, was the original foundation bed of river gravel and pottery shards laid by the village founders fifty years before!

Faced with undeniable archaeological and botanical evidence, the landholder turned pale and confessed his crime.
King Krishnadevaraya restored the stolen land to Mallesh, fined Bhupati one hundred gold coins, and had the boundary stone set permanently in iron-reinforced mortar.
The people celebrated Tenali Raman’s keen deductive eye, which saw truth buried beneath the surface of the earth.
moral: Greedy neighbors who shift boundary stones under the cover of night are caught by the patient memory of roots.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 97
summary: A greedy and heartless sweetmeat vendor named Halwai Ramu operated a grand confectionery shop in the busiest market of Vijayanagara, fryi...
full_text:
A greedy and heartless sweetmeat vendor named Halwai Ramu operated a grand confectionery shop in the busiest market of Vijayanagara, frying delicious jalebis, gulab jamuns, and ghee laddus in giant copper vats.
A penniless, starving orphan boy named Somu, who had not eaten for two days, stood outside the shop window on the dusty street, inhaling the sweet, fragrant aromas of melting sugar and cardamom wafting from the vats.

The cruel vendor noticed the boy standing there. He grabbed the orphan by his collar, dragged him into the street, and shouted:
'Pay me two silver coins this instant!'
The weeping boy cried: 'Master, I touched nothing! I have no money!'
The vendor yelled: 'Thou hast stood outside my shop for an hour, sniffing the sweet fragrance of my royal jalebis! The aroma of my sweets belongs to me! Pay for the smell, or go to the debtor’s dungeon!'

A crowd gathered, outraged by the vendor's cruelty.
Tenali Raman stepped out from the crowd:
'Release the boy, Halwai Ramu. The boy’s debt shall be paid in full before the entire marketplace!'

Tenali reached into his purse, took out ten bright silver coins, and placed them inside an empty brass water vessel.
Tenali held the brass pot close to the vendor’s right ear.
With a vigorous, rhythmic motion, Tenali shook the pot:
*‘JINGLE-CLINK-CLATTER! JINGLE-CLINK-CLATTER!’*

The coins bounced and chimed loudly inside the brass pot.
Tenali stopped, looked at the vendor, and asked:
'Didst thou hear that sound, Halwai Ramu?'
The vendor blinked: 'Yes, I heard the jingle of ten silver coins!'
Tenali asked: 'Was it a sweet, pleasant sound?'
The vendor nodded greedily: 'Very sweet!'

Tenali smiled with razor-sharp justice:
'Splendid! The account is settled in full!
The poor orphan boy enjoyed the **smell** of thy sweetmeats; and thou hast enjoyed the **sound** of my silver coins!
Neither did he eat thy sweets, nor shalt thou touch my money!
The smell has been paid for with the sound!
Now, take thy hands off the child, or I will have the Market Overseer inspect the quality of thy rancid ghee!'

The entire marketplace roared with triumphant cheers and laughter!
The vendor shrank back into his shop in utter humiliation.
Tenali bought a large box of fresh laddus, handed them to the hungry orphan boy along with two silver coins, proving that poetic justice turns greed into public laughter.
moral: Those who demand payment for the fragrance of food must be paid with the sound of money.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 98
summary: While traveling across the countryside toward Hampi, Tenali Raman sat comfortably in his bullock cart, driven by a faithful servant. Alon...
full_text:
While traveling across the countryside toward Hampi, Tenali Raman sat comfortably in his bullock cart, driven by a faithful servant. Along the dusty, sun-baked highway, Tenali noticed a weary traveler walking with bent shoulders, carrying an enormous, heavy sack of wheat upon his head. The man was sweating profusely, groaning with every step.

Moved by compassion, Tenali stopped the cart:
'Brother, thou art weary. Climb into my cart; we are traveling to the same city.'

The traveler thanked Tenali with tears of relief, climbed into the back of the wooden cart, and sat down upon the straw.
However, Tenali noticed that the man did not put down the heavy sack of wheat!
He continued balancing the massive sack upon his aching head, his neck muscles straining, sweat pouring into his eyes, gripping the burlap bag with both hands!

Tenali looked back in utter astonishment:
'Friend! Why art thou still carrying that heavy sack upon thy head?
Put it down upon the floor of the cart!'

The traveler replied with earnest, simple-minded concern:
'Noble master, you have been so kind to let me ride in your cart.
Your two bullocks are already pulling the weight of the cart, your servant, and myself.
I did not want to burden your poor bullocks with the extra weight of my heavy sack of wheat, so I decided to carry it upon my own head!'

Tenali Raman burst into gentle, affectionate laughter:
'O simple brother! Think for a moment!
Where art thou sitting?'
'In the cart, master.'
'And where is the cart resting?'
'Upon its wheels.'
'And who is pulling the cart and everything inside it?'
'The bullocks, master.'

Tenali smiled with deep philosophical warmth:
'Whether the sack rests upon the cart floor or upon thy head, the poor bullocks carry the exact same weight!
The only difference is that by keeping it on thy head, thou art breaking thy own neck for nothing!
Put down thy burden, rest thy weary back, and let the cart carry the load.'

The traveler realized the simple truth, placed the sack upon the straw, and breathed a deep sigh of relief.
Tenali turned to his servant and said:
'Look at human nature! We ride in the great cart of divine destiny, yet we carry the heavy sacks of our anxieties, worries, and fears upon our own heads, sweating and groaning, forgetting that the universe carries both us and our burdens together!'
moral: Worrying endlessly while carried by destiny is like carrying your luggage on your head while riding a bullock cart.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 99
summary: A formidable scholar from Kalinga named Mahadeva Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara. He was a master of palindromic poetry (*Ga...
full_text:
A formidable scholar from Kalinga named Mahadeva Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara. He was a master of palindromic poetry (*Gatagata-kavya*)—verses that read identically forward and backward, letter for letter, retaining poetic meter and philosophical meaning.
He challenged the court:
'Let any poet of Vijayanagara compose an eight-line classical verse praising the Emperor that reads identically forward and backward! If none can match me before noon, your court must surrender its poetic laurels!'

The royal poets struggled for hours. Crafting a single rhyming line forward and backward without creating gibberish was excruciatingly difficult.
King Krishnadevaraya looked anxiously at Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, composing verses that read forward and backward is child’s play in Vijayanagara.
In fact, my very name is a divine palindrome!'

The scholar frowned: 'Thy name?'
Tenali declared:
'Indeed! In our Telugu language, my name is written:
**VI - KA - TA - KA - VI** (The Jester-Poet)!
Read it forward: *VI-KA-TA-KA-VI*!
Read it backward: *VI-KA-TA-KA-VI*!
My name was born an eternal palindrome, before I ever wrote a single line of verse!'

Tenali then picked up an iron stylus and engraved an eight-line masterpiece upon a palm leaf.
The verse praised King Krishnadevaraya’s valor in war and benevolence in peace.
When read forward, it was a soaring hymn of royal victory;
When read backward, letter for letter, it formed an equally sublime hymn praising the King’s compassion and justice!

The scholar from Kalinga read the palm leaf forward, then backward, checking every syllable with trembling fingers.
He could not find a single flaw in meter, grammar, or sentiment.

The scholar bowed low, laid his gold-embroidered shawl at Tenali’s feet, and confessed:
'Tenali Raman, thou art truly *Vikatakavi*—a poet whose mind moves in all directions with peerless grace!'
King Krishnadevaraya rewarded Tenali with a chest of pearls, celebrating that true mastery wears its genius with lightness and joy.
moral: Intellectual vanity that seeks to defeat others through linguistic acrobatics is disarmed by simple wit.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 100
summary: A visiting puritanical ascetic persuaded King Krishnadevaraya that all forms of aromatic herbal pipe smoking (*hookah*) among the courtie...
full_text:
A visiting puritanical ascetic persuaded King Krishnadevaraya that all forms of aromatic herbal pipe smoking (*hookah*) among the courtiers was a sinful distraction from state duties.
Impulsively, the King issued a strict imperial decree:
'Henceforth, any citizen or courtier caught inhaling herbal smoke through a water pipe shall be publicly fined one hundred gold coins and marched through the streets on a backwards donkey!'

The decree caused great grumbling among aged ministers who found comfort in simple evening herbal tobacco after long hours of administration.

Tenali Raman resolved to show the King the absurdity of micromanaging the private habits of peaceful citizens.

The next morning, while King Krishnadevaraya was taking his morning walk through the royal gardens, he smelled a terrible, acrid stench of burning weeds coming from the imperial rose pavilion.
Rushing into the pavilion, the King stood frozen in shock:
Tenali Raman had constructed a massive, six-foot-tall water pipe using an enormous earthenware drainage jug, thirty feet of hollow bamboo tubing, and a smoking furnace of burning dry cow-dung and bitter neem leaves!
Tenali had the bamboo tube in his mouth, puffing furiously, clouds of thick, foul-smelling smoke billowing out across the royal roses!

The King coughed, waved the smoke away, and roared in fury:
'Tenali! Hast thou lost thy mind? Thou art violating my imperial decree inside my own private garden!'

Tenali coughed, bowed with watery eyes, and spoke:
'Maharaj! I am merely obeying your royal command with imperial magnificence!
You decreed that private herbal pipes are forbidden; so I built this public municipal pipe!
I am inhaling the medicinal smoke of cow-dung and neem to purify the palace air of harmful vapors!'

The King stared at the smoking monstrosity, then looked at Tenali’s soot-stained face.
Tenali added gently:
'Jahanpanah, a great Emperor governs the defense of the borders, the justice of the courts, and the feeding of the hungry.
When an Emperor begins regulating whether an old grandfather may smoke a mild herbal pipe on his own veranda at night, he wastes royal authority on trifles and turns his citizens into grumbling lawbreakers.
True temperance is taught through education, not through decrees on water pipes.'

King Krishnadevaraya saw the wisdom behind the smoke.
He laughed heartily, canceled the harsh prohibition, and advised moderation instead, proving that wise governance knows where the law ends and personal freedom begins.
moral: Excessive royal prohibitions that interfere with harmless private customs are cured through satirical demonstration.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 101
summary: A wealthy and selfish courtier named Ramabhadra discovered that King Krishnadevaraya had imported fifty rare, graft-bred mango saplings c...
full_text:
A wealthy and selfish courtier named Ramabhadra discovered that King Krishnadevaraya had imported fifty rare, graft-bred mango saplings capable of bearing sweet golden fruit twice a year.
Using his influence with the royal chief gardener, Ramabhadra bribed the staff, diverted all fifty saplings to his own private country estate, and left none for the public orchards!
When citizens inquired about the promised distribution, the corrupt gardener claimed: 'Alas! A blight of locusts ate all the saplings in the nursery!'

Tenali Raman suspected foul play.
He visited Ramabhadra’s estate disguised as a traveling soil chemist from Ujjain.
Walking through the private walled orchard, Tenali saw the fifty rare saplings planted in neat, irrigated rows, thriving with green shoots.

Tenali returned to the palace and whispered to King Krishnadevaraya:
'Maharaj, a rare and miraculous golden herb grows in Ramabhadra's orchard! Its leaves possess the supernatural power to double the yield of all fruit trees in the kingdom, but only if they are transplanted into the communal fields within three days!'

The King, accompanied by his ministers and Tenali, rode unannounced to Ramabhadra’s estate.
When the gates opened, the King was shocked to see all fifty of his imported royal mango saplings growing in Ramabhadra's private soil!
The King’s brow darkened with thunder:
'Ramabhadra! The chief gardener told me these saplings were eaten by locusts! Art thou the two-legged locust who ate the royal nursery?'

Ramabhadra fell to his knees in terror, begging for mercy.
Tenali smiled and said:
'Maharaj, let the punishment fit the crime!
Ramabhadra loved these saplings so dearly that he must be granted the honor of planting them!
Order Ramabhadra to dig up all fifty saplings with his own hands, carry them on his own shoulders to the public gardens of the weavers' quarter, replant them in the communal soil, and water them every dawn for one full year!'

The King approved the verdict with a hearty laugh.
The proud, wealthy courtier was stripped of his fine silks, handed a spade, and spent the entire year digging holes and carrying water buckets for the poor weavers.
The mango saplings flourished, yielding sweet fruit for hundreds of children, proving that public blessings belong to the community, not to the greed of a few.
moral: Greed that tries to corner agricultural blessings is cured when made to tend the soil of the poor.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 102
summary: In the court of Vijayanagara, a senior councilor named Bhupati Rao was notorious for his shameless flattery. When the King wore a blue co...
full_text:
In the court of Vijayanagara, a senior councilor named Bhupati Rao was notorious for his shameless flattery. When the King wore a blue coat, Bhupati declared: 'Blue is the only divine color of kings!' If the King changed to green the next day, Bhupati exclaimed: 'Green is the supreme color of cosmic glory; blue is fit only for peasants!'
The courtiers laughed behind their sleeves, but none dared challenge the sycophant openly.

Tenali Raman decided to cure the courtier before the entire diwan.
Tenali commissioned a skilled metalworker to cast a bronze hand mirror with a subtle, concave distortion: looking straight into the center showed a man with an enormous, puffed-out chin and tiny, squinting eyes!

The next morning, during a discussion on military uniforms, the King asked:
'What think you, councilors? Should our cavalry wear crimson turbans or saffron dhotis?'
Bhupati Rao immediately leaped forward:
'Crimson, Maharaj! Crimson is the color of eternal victory! Saffron is weak and dull!'

Tenali Raman stepped up beside the courtier, holding up the distorted bronze mirror directly in front of Bhupati’s face:
'Look into this mirror, Bhupati Rao! What magnificent statesman dost thou behold?'

Bhupati glanced into the mirror, saw his absurdly puffed-out chin, bulging cheeks, and tiny squinting eyes, and gasped:
'Heavens! Who is this hideous, bloated monster in the bronze?'

Tenali Raman turned the mirror toward the King and addressed the court:
'Maharaj, this is the Mirror of the Flatterer’s Soul!
Just as this bronze glass bends and distorts reality to reflect whatever ugly shape the curve dictates, so too Bhupati’s tongue bends and twists with every breath from the throne!
Yesterday he praised blue, today he praises crimson, and tomorrow he will praise mud if Your Majesty smiles upon a ditch!
A man whose words have no backbone is like a warped mirror: he reflects only distorted nonsense!'

The entire audience erupted in roaring laughter!
King Krishnadevaraya chuckled heartily, nodding in agreement.
Bhupati Rao turned bright crimson, lowered his head in utter humiliation, and quietly slunk to the back row.
He never again offered contradictory flattery, while Tenali showed that consistency and honesty are the true jewels of courtly advice.
moral: A flatterer's tongue changes with every shift in power; holding up the mirror of consistency shames the hypocrite.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 103
summary: Two timber merchants from the Malabar border, Keshav and Madhav, appeared before King Krishnadevaraya's court, dragging a playful young e...
full_text:
Two timber merchants from the Malabar border, Keshav and Madhav, appeared before King Krishnadevaraya's court, dragging a playful young elephant calf on a rope. Both men claimed ownership of the calf.
Keshav swore: 'The calf was born to my working cow-elephant, Lakshmi, six months ago! Madhav stole it from my forest corral!'
Madhav shouted: 'Liar! It was born to my cow-elephant, Gauri, in the river valley! I have three witnesses who saw the birth!'

Because both merchants presented stamped sales certificates and sworn witnesses, the royal judges were completely divided.
The King turned to Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, settle this dispute, for the judges cannot read the minds of elephants.'

Tenali smiled: 'Maharaj, the court of humans may be confused by forged seals, but the court of nature knows no perjury.
Order both cow-elephants, Lakshmi and Gauri, brought to the royal parade grounds immediately.'

The two mother elephants were brought to opposite sides of the vast arena, held by their mahouts fifty paces apart.
The young calf was placed in the exact center of the dusty field, untied and free.

Tenali commanded both merchants: 'Call your elephants, and let the mothers call their child!'

Madhav shouted commands, and his elephant Gauri flapped her ears indifferently, looking toward the river, chewing sugarcane.
Then Keshav spoke gentle, rhythmic words in the forest dialect.
His elephant Lakshmi lifted her trunk high into the air and let out a soft, deep, rumbling maternal trumpet of profound longing!

The moment the little calf heard Lakshmi’s rumble, its ears perked up!
The calf ignored Madhav’s elephant completely, let out a joyous squeal, and galloped as fast as its stubby legs could carry it across the sand!
It ran straight to Lakshmi, ducked beneath her belly, nuzzled against her front leg, and began nursing greedily!
Lakshmi wrapped her great trunk tenderly around the calf's back, caressing its ears with maternal adoration!

Tenali turned to the King and the assembly:
'Look, Maharaj! No calf ever nurses from a stranger, nor does a mother elephant caress another’s offspring with such tender devotion!
Nature has delivered the verdict: the calf belongs to Keshav!'

The assembly cheered the undeniable truth of nature.
Madhav was fined fifty gold coins for theft and perjury, Keshav was reunited with his elephants, and King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali’s profound understanding of maternal instinct.
moral: Nature's maternal bonds cannot be deceived by forged sales deeds; the mother's heart identifies her true offspring.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 104
summary: A haughty scholar of Nyaya (formal logic) named Tarka Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that his mastery of syllogis...
full_text:
A haughty scholar of Nyaya (formal logic) named Tarka Shastri arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that his mastery of syllogistic reasoning could prove anything in the universe, true or false.
Before King Krishnadevaraya, he argued:
'Maharaj, observe my flawless logical deduction:
Major Premise: All cats have four legs.
Minor Premise: My wooden dining table has four legs.
Conclusion: Therefore, my wooden dining table is an authentic living cat!
None can challenge the mathematical structure of formal logic!'

The courtiers looked baffled. While they knew the conclusion was absurd, none could untangle the philosophical sophistry.
King Krishnadevaraya was amused, but annoyed by the scholar's arrogance.

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, Tarka Shastri’s logic is truly magnificent!
In fact, I have applied his exact philosophical syllogism to solve the palace dairy shortage!'

Tenali ordered a servant to bring a large clay bowl filled with rich, creamy white curd from the royal kitchens.
Tenali placed the bowl upon the scholar’s wooden table.
Tenali then turned to Tarka Shastri:
'Revered logician, since you have proven beyond dispute that your wooden dining table is an authentic living cat, let us observe its feline behavior!
Cats love nothing more than sweet milk and fresh curd.
Command your wooden table to lap up this bowl of curd!
If your table is a real cat, it will eat with pleasure. But if it fails to eat, your logic is nothing more than empty sophistry!'

The scholar stood frozen, staring at the motionless wooden table and the bowl of curd.
The court waited in silence.
One minute passed. Five minutes passed.
The wooden table, of course, did not move a single leg, nor did it lap up a drop of curd.

Tenali smiled with devastating wit:
'What is the matter, Master Logician? Is your table-cat feeling shy?
Or perhaps it prefers mice to curd?
A four-legged table remains dead timber, no matter how many clever words you spin to call it a cat!
When logic divorces itself from common sense and practical reality, it becomes the pastime of fools!'

King Krishnadevaraya and the entire court erupted in roaring laughter!
The haughty logician turned red with embarrassment, bowed his head, and conceded defeat.
The King awarded the bowl of sweet curd to Tenali Raman, celebrating that common sense is the master of all formal philosophy.
moral: Clever philosophical syllogisms that twist words to justify absurdities collapse when applied to practical life.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 105
summary: A traveling showman named Mayadas set up a colorful tent on the banks of the Tungabhadra River, displaying a large glass tank containing ...
full_text:
A traveling showman named Mayadas set up a colorful tent on the banks of the Tungabhadra River, displaying a large glass tank containing an enormous silver river carp.
He proclaimed to the crowds:
'Behold the Miraculous Singing Fish of the Saraswati!
When I play my flute, this sacred fish surfaces, opens its mouth, and sings ancient hymns in a sweet, melodious soprano voice!'

Citizens paid silver coins to enter.
Mayadas played his flute, the silver carp swam to the glass, opened and closed its mouth in rhythm—and indeed, a clear, sweet soprano voice filled the tent, singing beautiful melodies!
The citizens were spellbound, dropping gold and silver into the charity bowl.
Even several ministers reported to King Krishnadevaraya that a celestial reincarnation had appeared in the river.

Tenali Raman visited the tent, accompanied by his young nephew.
Tenali watched the tank intently.
He noticed that the fish opened and closed its mouth naturally to breathe water through its gills, matching the tempo of the flute.
He also noticed that the water in the glass tank showed zero acoustic ripples or vibrations while the song was being sung!
A voice powerful enough to fill a large tent should create circular sound ripples upon the surface of still water!

Tenali walked around the tent.
Behind the display platform stood a large, ornate wooden wardrobe draped in heavy red velvet curtains, supposedly containing 'ceremonial water jugs'.
Tenali gently took out a small hollow reed blowpipe from his sash, loaded it with a tiny pinch of fine black pepper, and blew it through a small seam in the back of the velvet wardrobe!

Within ten seconds, a violent, desperate sneeze erupted from inside the wardrobe:
*‘ACHOOO! ACHO0-OOF! COUGH!’*
And the 'singing fish' in the tank was suddenly interrupted mid-verse by an unmistakable, very human cough coming from inside the furniture!

Tenali pulled aside the heavy velvet curtain and swung open the wardrobe door:
Crouched inside upon a stool, holding a polished brass acoustic speaking-tube that funneled sound directly beneath the fish tank, was Mayadas’s sixteen-year-old sister, wiping her streaming eyes and coughing from the pepper!

The crowd gasped in outrage at the exposed deception!
The showman fell to the floor, begging Tenali for mercy.
Tenali smiled:
'Fish swim and breathe, but they do not sing in soprano!
Whenever you hear an impossible voice coming from a creature that has no vocal cords, search behind the nearest velvet curtain!'

The showman was ordered to refund all coins to the citizens, and Tenali’s sharp observational logic was celebrated across Vijayanagara.
moral: Supernatural marvels that extract money from the public are exposed when their hidden acoustics are traced.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 106
summary: A priceless uncut blue diamond from the mines of Golconda, kept in the King’s private gemological cabinet, vanished during an inventory a...
full_text:
A priceless uncut blue diamond from the mines of Golconda, kept in the King’s private gemological cabinet, vanished during an inventory audit.
The room had three keys, held by the three Chief Vault Keepers: Somadatta, Bheema, and Ramanathan.
All three men were searched immediately: their clothes, their shoes, and their lockers contained nothing.
All three swore upon their sacred threads that they were innocent.

King Krishnadevaraya, desperate to recover the crown jewel, called Tenali Raman.
Tenali said: 'Maharaj, the thief had no time to carry the diamond outside the palace walls, for the alarm was sounded within ten minutes of the theft.
The diamond is still hidden within this room.
Give me until midnight, and the thief will deliver the gem into my hand.'

Tenali had the room locked from the outside, leaving the three keepers inside with food and water.
Tenali had a small, concealed peephole drilled through the wooden ceiling beam, allowing him to watch the room from the attic above.

At midnight, Tenali leaned through the peephole and whispered in a low, mysterious, spectral tone that echoed through the stone chamber:
'Somadatta... Bheema... Ramanathan...
The King has ordered the master masons to arrive at dawn with sledgehammers!
They will break open the stone floor, dismantle the fireplace, and smash the carved wooden pillars to find the diamond!
Whoever hid the diamond behind the hollow brick in the hearth will see it found and lose his head!'

The three keepers leaped up from their cots in the dark.
Two of the keepers sat back down, confused by the strange voice.
However, the third keeper, Ramanathan, turned pale with terror!
He thought: 'Heavens! How did the King discover my secret hiding place behind the hearth?'

Panicking in the dark, Ramanathan crept silently to the large stone fireplace.
He reached his hand up the chimney flue, pulled away a loose soot-covered brick, took out the blue diamond wrapped in wax paper, and tried to slip it into his turban!

At that moment, Tenali Raman kicked open the heavy door, carrying a bright lantern and backed by royal guards!
'Hold, Ramanathan! Thou hast found the diamond for us!'

Ramanathan dropped the soot-covered gem, falling to his knees in utter confession.
The King was amazed at how Tenali’s phantom whisper had caused the thief to unmask his own cache.
The Golconda diamond was restored to the crown, Ramanathan was sentenced to restorative labor, and Tenali was rewarded with a gold medallion for his brilliant psychological deduction.
moral: A thief's secret stash is unearthed when suspicion is cast upon the only man who knows the hiding place.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 107
summary: An arrogant foreign king, seeking an excuse to declare war upon Vijayanagara without appearing aggressive, sent an impossible diplomatic ...
full_text:
An arrogant foreign king, seeking an excuse to declare war upon Vijayanagara without appearing aggressive, sent an impossible diplomatic ultimatum to King Krishnadevaraya:
'To our brother Krishnadevaraya:
We demand that your famous engineers dig an abundant, fresh-water stone well atop the highest, sharpest rocky granite peak of Mount Matanga within thirty days, so that our passing caravans may drink!
If you fail, we shall consider your empire negligent of regional trade and declare war!'

The King’s master masons and hydrologists were in despair:
'Maharaj, Mount Matanga is a solid, towering pyramid of barren granite! There are no underground aquifers on a peak two thousand cubits above the valley! To dig a well there is an absolute impossibility!'

King Krishnadevaraya sat with a heavy heart, dreading an unjust war.
Tenali Raman stepped forward with a smile:
'Maharaj, reply to the foreign king that his royal request has been enthusiastically accepted, and that I, Tenali Raman, shall personally lay the foundation stone of the well on Mount Matanga!'

Two weeks later, Tenali Raman arrived as an imperial envoy at the foreign king's palace.
Tenali bowed with majestic courtly elegance and announced:
'Your Majesty! Emperor Krishnadevaraya has mobilized five hundred stone masons, twenty water diviners, and three hundred bullocks to construct your magnificent well atop Mount Matanga!
The summit has been surveyed, and the sacred coordinates are marked!'

The foreign king was stunned: 'Truly? You have begun digging into solid granite?'
Tenali replied with immense enthusiasm:
'Indeed! But as Your Majesty knows, our ancient architectural treatises state that a well dug upon a high mountain peak cannot stand unless its foundation is anchored with **Mountain-Base Granite Clay** supplied by the requesting monarch!
We have brought fifty pack-camels to your gates.
I pray thee, Your Majesty: order your servants to shovel three hundred cartloads of Mountain-Base Granite Clay from the sky into our sacks, so we may lay the foundation of your well tomorrow morning!'

The foreign king stared in bewilderment:
'Shovel granite clay from the sky? Art thou mad? How can anyone shovel stone from empty air?'

Tenali smiled with dazzling, razor-sharp wit:
'Precisely, Your Majesty!
If your kingdom cannot shovel granite clay from empty clouds, how can Vijayanagara dig an aquifer well atop a barren mountain peak?
When a king makes an impossible demand to manufacture an excuse for war, he must provide the impossible materials to build his folly!'

The foreign king realized he had been completely outmatched in intellect and diplomacy.
He laughed in admiration, withdrew his ultimatum, and signed a perpetual treaty of peace with Vijayanagara, while Tenali returned home having averted a war with a handful of wit.
moral: Demands to perform impossible geographic feats are countered by requiring the impossible foundation stones to begin.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 108
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, inflamed by a false intelligence report that a neighboring border governor had insulted the royal standard, leaped ...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, inflamed by a false intelligence report that a neighboring border governor had insulted the royal standard, leaped up from his throne in a fiery rage.
He drew his sword and shouted to his generals:
'Mobilize ten thousand cavalry immediately! We march at sunset to burn the governor’s citadel and put his garrison to the sword!'

Prime Minister Appaji and the senior ministers were terrified: they knew the border governor was loyal, and that the report was a deceptive rumor spread by enemy spies to provoke a destructive war.
Yet none dared speak against the King while his wrath was boiling.

Tenali Raman stepped forward, carrying a large brass pot of fresh, thick milk and an open charcoal brazier.
Tenali placed the brazier on the floor before the throne, set the pot of milk upon the coals, and blew the embers until they glowed red-hot.

Within minutes, the milk began to boil violently.
White foam rose rapidly up the sides of the brass pot, threatening to boil over and spill across the King's velvet throne carpet!
The King shouted in annoyance:
'Tenali! Look at the milk! It is boiling over! Take it off the fire before it ruins the carpet!'

Tenali stood calmly with folded hands, doing nothing.
The King leaped up, reached for a jug of cold water, and splashed three drops of cold water into the bubbling foam:
Instantly, the white foam subsided, the boiling quieted, and the milk settled peacefully inside the pot!

Tenali smiled with profound gentleness:
'Look, Maharaj!
When the milk was boiling violently with fiery heat, a single cup of cold water was enough to restore calm and save the carpet.
Your royal mind is currently boiling with the fiery heat of anger from an unverified rumor.
If you march your army today while your wrath is foaming, you will spill the blood of hundreds of innocent soldiers and ruin the carpet of your empire!
Pour three drops of cold patience upon your boiling heart. Wait three days. Verify the report.
If the governor is truly a traitor, your sword can strike him down on the fourth day just as easily as today.
But if you strike in haste, not all the tears in the world can bring a slain loyal servant back to life.'

King Krishnadevaraya looked at the settled milk, then at his drawn sword.
The fever of anger broke.
The King sheathed his weapon: 'Tenali, thy pot of milk has saved an empire from folly.'

Three days later, messengers arrived with proof that the report was an enemy forgery! The loyal border governor was innocent.
The King embraced Tenali, acknowledging that patience is the true shield of a righteous ruler.
moral: Haste and anger ruin the finest plans; patient waiting allows boiling fury to cool into wisdom.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 109
summary: A notoriously stingy landlord named Kuberappa was embarrassed by his reputation as a miser. To improve his social standing, he invited al...
full_text:
A notoriously stingy landlord named Kuberappa was embarrassed by his reputation as a miser. To improve his social standing, he invited all the scholars, poets, and councilors of Vijayanagara, including Tenali Raman, to an 'Imperial Eight-Course Banquet' at his grand mansion.

The guests arrived, their mouths watering in anticipation.
They were seated upon silk cushions around an empty dining hall.
Kuberappa entered, clapped his hands with theatrical enthusiasm, and said:
'Welcome, noble guests! Let the feast begin!
Imagine, my friends! Look at the imaginary silver platters before you!
Behold this celestial saffron rice cooked in pure ghee! Inhale its divine aroma!
Taste these imaginary almond laddus, crisp samosas, and roasted partridges!
Eat, my friends, eat of the feast of imagination!'

The bewildered guests sat in stunned silence with empty plates.
While the other scholars frowned in angry disgust, Tenali Raman smiled with supreme enthusiasm!
Tenali pretended to scoop up imaginary rice with his fingers, smacking his lips with loud relish:
'Ah! Divine! Magnificent! Kuberappa, your imaginary samosas are crispy, and your imaginary payasam is sweeter than nectar!'
Tenali chewed the empty air, swallowed imaginary sweets, and rubbed his stomach with theatrical joy:
'I have never eaten so well in all my life!'

Kuberappa was delighted, thinking Tenali was supporting his cheap trick.

As the gathering concluded, Kuberappa accompanied the guests to the front gate.
Tenali Raman turned to Kuberappa, bowed low, and reached into his pocket.
Tenali pulled out an empty fist, held it over Kuberappa’s open palm, and pantomimed dropping fifty heavy gold coins into the landlord's hand:
'Here, noble Kuberappa! Take this generous tip of fifty imaginary gold coins for your magnificent feast!
Feel their heavy, glittering weight! Buy yourself fifty imaginary cows and an imaginary palace of marble!'

Kuberappa stared at his completely empty hand:
'Tenali! My hand is empty! You have given me nothing!'

Tenali laughed with booming joy:
'Why, noble host! If an imaginary saffron banquet can fill the bellies of twenty hungry scholars, surely fifty imaginary gold coins will fill your treasury to overflowing!
You fed us on empty air, and I have paid you with phantom gold!
The account is balanced to the last coin!'

The entire gathering burst into roaring laughter, while Kuberappa turned red as a beet.
Humiliated by the lesson, Kuberappa rushed to his kitchen, ordered his cooks to light the fires, and served the guests an actual, lavish feast of real rice, ghee, and sweets, learning that hospitality must be real to earn real honor.
moral: Miserly hosts who promise grand banquets but serve empty airs deserve to feast on imaginary fragrances.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 110
summary: The King’s chief royal falconer, an arrogant man named Shaukat, boasted that his prize hunting falcon, Toofan, was the fiercest, fastest ...
full_text:
The King’s chief royal falconer, an arrogant man named Shaukat, boasted that his prize hunting falcon, Toofan, was the fiercest, fastest predator in the skies. He trained his birds through starvation and harsh whipping, mocking the palace pigeon-keepers who raised gentle homing doves.
Shaukat boasted:
'Gentle birds are cowards! Only beasts ruled by fear and hunger possess true skill!
My falcon can intercept and bring down any bird in Vijayanagara within two minutes of release!'

Tenali Raman smiled:
'Shaukat, love and gentle patience build stronger wings than cruelty and starvation.
I wager that a simple, gentle homing dove raised with affection can outfly your fiercest falcon!'

The wager was accepted before King Krishnadevaraya on the palace terraces.
Shaukat brought forward his fierce falcon, hooded, talons sharpened, screeching hungrily.
Tenali brought a modest, snow-white homing dove named Shanti, which perched calmly upon his wrist, cooing affectionately and pecking sweet millet from his palm.

The signal was given!
Tenali released the white dove into the sky.
Shaukat unhooded his fierce falcon, shouting: 'Strike, Toofan! Slay the dove!'
The falcon soared into the air with lightning speed, its talons extended, diving directly at the white dove!

Any ordinary bird would have panicked and fluttered into the open air to be shredded.
However, Tenali had trained the dove through patient love: whenever danger appeared, the dove knew that safety lay in diving straight into the deep, thorny bougainvillea trellis on the palace terrace!
The dove folded its wings, plummeted like a white stone, and darted safely into the dense, maze-like thorns of the thick bougainvillea bush!

The fierce falcon, blinded by aggressive hunger and flying too fast to pull up, crashed headlong into the dense, thorny brambles!
Its wings were tangled, its feathers plucked, and it struggled helplessly among the thorns, squawking in panic!

Tenali gently reached his hand into the safe inner hollow of the bush:
The little white dove hopped calmly onto his fingers, completely unhurt, cooing softly!

Tenali freed the tangled falcon, smoothed its bruised feathers, and handed it back to the humiliated falconer:
'Look, Shaukat! Thy falcon was driven by blind, starving fury, and crashed into ruin.
My dove was guided by calm trust and loving intelligence, finding safe refuge in an instant!
Cruelty blinds the eyes, but patience and gentle affection conquer the skies.'

The King praised Tenali’s gentle wisdom, awarded him the prize, and ordered the royal falconry to abandon harsh training methods in favor of humane care.
moral: Cruelty and arrogance toward gentle creatures are defeated by patient training and natural devotion.
