title: Tenali Raman Tale 140
summary: Two neighboring householders, Somu and Ramu, were locked in a bitter feud over a massive coconut palm tree. The trunk of the tree grew in...
full_text:
Two neighboring householders, Somu and Ramu, were locked in a bitter feud over a massive coconut palm tree.
The trunk of the tree grew in Somu’s garden, but its top branches leaned over the wall, hanging directly above Ramu’s tiled roof.
Whenever ripe coconuts fell, they smashed Ramu’s roof tiles; but whenever Ramu picked the fallen coconuts, Somu accused him of theft!
Somu claimed: 'The roots are in my soil; every coconut belongs to me!'
Ramu claimed: 'The nuts fall on my roof and break my tiles; they belong to me!'

They brought the dispute to King Krishnadevaraya, demanding that the tree either be chopped down or the other neighbor imprisoned.
The King referred the case to Tenali Raman.

Tenali inspected the coconut tree.
He said to both men:
'The law must divide the tree according to natural equity!
Since Somu owns the trunk and roots in his soil, Somu shall be the sole owner of the **lower half** of the tree from the roots up to the branches!
And since Ramu owns the airspace and suffers the broken tiles, Ramu shall be the sole owner of the **upper half** of the tree where the coconuts grow!'

Both men were delighted:
Ramu smiled, thinking he would get all the coconuts;
Somu smiled, thinking he owned the base.

Then Tenali announced the operational rules:
'Now, hear the law:
Somu, as owner of the lower trunk, must water the roots, fertilize the soil, and protect the trunk every single day! But he is strictly forbidden from climbing into Ramu’s upper half to touch a single coconut!
And Ramu, as owner of the upper half, may harvest all the coconuts! But he is strictly forbidden from touching Somu’s trunk with a ladder or stepping upon Somu’s bark to climb up!'

The two neighbors stared at each other in stunned silence.
Somu realized: 'If I water the tree, Ramu gets all the coconuts, and I get only hard labor!'
Ramu realized: 'If I cannot touch the trunk or lean a ladder against it, I cannot reach the coconuts at all!'

Tenali looked at them with a warm, gentle smile:
'Do you see the folly of your stubborn selfishness?
Nature created a tree as a single, harmonious living blessing. You cannot divide a living tree with anger without rendering it useless to both!
Now, shake hands:
Let Somu water the tree, let Ramu harvest the coconuts, and let both families share the sweet fruit equally, dividing the coconuts and sharing the cost of repairing the roof tiles!'

The two neighbors were deeply moved by Tenali’s wise counsel.
They embraced, dropped their lawsuits, and shared the harvests for decades in harmony and peace.
moral: Generosity and neighborly compromise yield sweet fruit; selfish litigation bears only legal thorns.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 141
summary: An elderly, impoverished court copyist named Shastriji dropped his worn, ancient iron writing stylus (*ghantam*) into the deep palace wat...
full_text:
An elderly, impoverished court copyist named Shastriji dropped his worn, ancient iron writing stylus (*ghantam*) into the deep palace water reservoir.
The stylus was thirty years old, its wooden grip worn smooth by decades of copying sacred scriptures and imperial decrees.
Shastriji sat on the stone steps of the reservoir, weeping bitterly, unable to earn his daily bread without his writing tool.

Tenali Raman saw the old scholar weeping and dove into the clear, deep water.
Tenali surfaced holding a magnificent stylus crafted of solid, gleaming twenty-four-karat gold, encrusted with rubies!
'Is this thy writing stylus, Shastriji?' asked Tenali.

Old Shastriji looked at the dazzling golden tool, blinked through his tears, and shook his head with simple honesty:
'No, noble Tenali. That golden stylus belongs to a king or an emperor.
Gold is too soft and slippery to carve fine letters upon dry palm leaves; my fingers would slip.
My stylus was a plain tool of hardened iron, with a humble handle of neem wood smoothed by thirty years of honest ink.'

Tenali dove a second time, surfacing with an ornate stylus of pure, polished silver with an ivory handle:
'Is this thine?'
Shastriji replied: 'No, master. Silver tarnishes, and its tip is too blunt for my delicate script. That is not mine.'

Tenali dove a third time, bringing up Shastriji’s old, blackened iron stylus with its worn neem handle.
The old scribe let out a cry of pure, joyous relief, clutching the iron tool to his chest as though it were his own child:
'Yes! That is my stylus! That is the breadwinner of my family! With this iron tip, I have copied ten thousand pages of poetry!'

Tenali Raman was moved to tears by the old scribe’s profound, incorruptible honesty and love for his craft.
Tenali presented Shastriji with his old iron stylus, and then handed him the gold and silver styluses as gifts, along with a purse of fifty gold coins from King Krishnadevaraya:
'Shastriji, an honest craftsman who honors the humble tools of his labor is greater than an emperor.
Take the gold to secure thy family’s comfort, and use thine iron stylus to continue copying the wisdom of our ancestors!'

The old scribe blessed Tenali with a full heart, proving that true wealth resides in honest devotion to one’s work.
moral: Honest tools used with devotion are the true wealth of a craftsman; false pride seeks only golden toys.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 142
summary: A sudden panic struck the northern agricultural district of Anegundi: A rumor spread that an ancient curse had turned the communal irriga...
full_text:
A sudden panic struck the northern agricultural district of Anegundi:
A rumor spread that an ancient curse had turned the communal irrigation lake completely salty!
Farmers tasted the water at the southern weir and spat it out in horror: it was intensely salty, threatening to kill their rice crops!
A corrupt grain speculator named Bhupati immediately offered to buy all the farmers’ lands at pennies on the dollar, claiming the valley was ruined forever.

King Krishnadevaraya sent Tenali Raman to investigate the catastrophe.

Tenali rode to the lake.
He tasted the water at the southern weir: indeed, it was intensely salty.
However, Tenali rowed a small wooden boat across to the northern inlet where the mountain mountain stream entered the lake:
He dipped his cup into the water:
The northern inlet water was completely, delightfully sweet, fresh, and cold!

Tenali reasoned:
'If a curse had salted the lake, the entire body of water would be uniformly saline.
Why is the water fresh at the northern inlet, but salty only at the southern weir?'

Tenali inspected the stone masonry of the southern weir.
Beneath the water line, Tenali’s boat paddle struck something soft.
He dove into the shallows:
Submerged behind the stone sluice gate were thirty enormous burlap sacks of coarse sea salt, slowly dissolving into the outflow current!
Tied to the sacks was an iron tag stamped with the warehouse seal of none other than **Grain Speculator Bhupati**!

Bhupati had dumped thirty cartloads of cheap sea salt into the weir to create a temporary panic, hoping to buy the fertile lands for nothing!

Tenali hauled the salt sacks out of the water, arrested Bhupati on the spot, and had the sluice gate flushed with fresh mountain water.
Within two hours, the outflow ran completely sweet and fresh again!
The farmers cheered, their lands were saved, and Bhupati’s entire grain empire was confiscated to fund free agricultural schools.
King Krishnadevaraya praised Tenali Raman’s sharp scientific logic, which saw through speculative fraud to protect the innocent.
moral: False rumors designed to spark speculative panics are extinguished by scientific investigation.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 143
summary: A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Somadatta was murdered and robbed of five hundred gold coins in an alley behind the Great Shiva ...
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Vijayanagara named Somadatta was murdered and robbed of five hundred gold coins in an alley behind the Great Shiva Temple.
A notorious rogue named Shankara was arrested as the primary suspect, having been seen near the temple.
However, Shankara produced a sworn witness, an astrologer named Keshava, who swore an oath before the court:
'Shankara is innocent! At the exact hour of the murder—precisely two hours after sunrise on Friday morning—Shankara was sitting with me on the eastern steps of the temple, resting in the cool shadow of the temple spire, studying his horoscope!'

Because the alibi was supported by a respected astrologer, the court was on the verge of releasing Shankara.
Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, let us examine the astrologer’s astronomical testimony.'

Tenali turned to Keshava:
'Revered Astrologer, you swear that you and Shankara were resting in the shadow of the great temple spire on the **eastern steps** two hours after sunrise?'
Keshava puffed out his chest: 'I swear it upon the sacred scriptures! The shadow was cool and dark upon our heads!'

Tenali Raman burst into laughter:
'Maharaj! The alibi is a fabricated, perjured lie!'
The King demanded: 'How dost thou know, Tenali?'

Tenali explained the basic laws of solar geometry:
'The sun rises in the **East**!
Two hours after sunrise, the morning sun is climbing high in the eastern sky!
Therefore, the shadow of any building, pillar, or temple spire falls toward the **WEST**!
The eastern steps of the temple were bathed in blazing, direct morning sunlight!
The shadow of the temple spire could not possibly fall upon the eastern steps; it fell upon the western garden!
Only a liar who was never there would claim to sit in a western shadow on an eastern staircase!'

The astrologer’s knees buckled in terror. He confessed that Shankara had bribed him with fifty gold coins to fabricate the alibi.
Shankara broke down, confessed the murder, and led the guards to the stolen gold.
King Krishnadevaraya embraced Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, while lawyers argue words, thou dost call upon the sun itself to testify to the truth!'
Justice was delivered, and Tenali’s astronomical deduction was hailed throughout the empire.
moral: A liar who invents a false alibi is trapped by the immutable physics of the sun.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 144
summary: An elderly scholar named Ramakrishna Shastri purchased a fine, hand-woven Benares silk turban dyed with rare vegetable indigo, embroidere...
full_text:
An elderly scholar named Ramakrishna Shastri purchased a fine, hand-woven Benares silk turban dyed with rare vegetable indigo, embroidered with tiny silver lotus motifs along the border.
While taking a bath at the public river ghat, he left the turban on a flat stone.
A haughty courtier named Somappa snatched the turban and wrapped it around his own head.
When the poor scholar confronted him, Somappa sneered:
'Old beggar! This turban is an ancestral heirloom of my noble family! How dare a threadbare scholar claim my silk?'

The dispute was brought before Tenali Raman.
Somappa produced three friends who swore the turban had belonged to his family for years.
The poor scholar wept, having no witnesses.

Tenali Raman looked at the disputed silk turban.
He asked Somappa: 'What thread was used to stitch the inner lining of this turban?'
Somappa guessed: 'Fine silver thread, of course!'
Tenali asked the scholar: 'What thread was used?'
The scholar answered:
'Because I am poor, my wife stitched the inner headband with coarse, blue cotton thread, and inside the seam she placed a small dried jasmine leaf for fragrance.'

Tenali carefully snipped two stitches of the inner lining before the court:
Inside was coarse blue cotton thread, and between the silk folds lay a single, dried, fragrant jasmine leaf!

Tenali smiled:
'Somappa, you know the price of silk, but only the poor scholar’s wife knows the humble thread that binds it!'

Somappa was fined fifty gold coins for theft and perjury, which were awarded to the scholar, and the silk turban was restored to its rightful owner.
The court praised Tenali Raman’s gentle, observant justice.
moral: Careful examination of the smallest details exposes the claims of arrogant thieves.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 145
summary: An envoy from the Chola kingdom of the south arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting three deep philosophical questions from his...
full_text:
An envoy from the Chola kingdom of the south arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, presenting three deep philosophical questions from his king:
'First: Who is the richest man in the world?
Second: Who is the poorest man in the world?
Third: Who is the most invincible warrior in the universe?'

The court ministers gave conventional answers:
'The richest is the Emperor with the most gold; the poorest is the beggar in rags; the most invincible is the general with the largest army!'
The Chola envoy shook his head: 'Those are common answers of common minds.'

Tenali Raman stepped forward:
'Maharaj, allow me to answer the Chola King’s inquiry.'

Tenali addressed the envoy:
'First: The **richest man in the world** is he who is completely content with what he has, who desires no more than what honest labor provides, and whose heart is free from envy! A contented man possesses the wealth of the universe!'

The envoy smiled: 'And who is the poorest?'
Tenali continued:
'Second: The **poorest man in the world** is the greedy king or miser who owns mountains of gold, yet tosses awake at night tormented by the craving for more! His soul is a bottomless pit of starvation, and no wealth can ever satisfy his spiritual poverty!'

The envoy nodded with deep reverence: 'And who is the most invincible warrior?'
Tenali concluded:
'Third: The **most invincible warrior in the universe** is not he who conquers ten thousand enemies with sword and lance, but he who conquers his own anger, his own pride, and his own selfish desires!
He who has conquered himself can never be defeated by any earthly foe!'

The Chola envoy was moved to tears by the sublime spiritual depth of Tenali’s answers.
He bowed low, presented Tenali with a golden medallion of honor, and declared:
'Emperor Krishnadevaraya, your empire is truly invincible, for it is guided by the wisdom of Tenali Raman!'
The King embraced Tenali, celebrating that moral truth outshines all earthly power.
moral: True royalty is defined by benevolence, true wisdom by humility, and true strength by self-mastery.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 146
summary: A cunning alchemist named Siddha Ramanand set up a laboratory in Vijayanagara, claiming he had perfected a secret clay crucible that coul...
full_text:
A cunning alchemist named Siddha Ramanand set up a laboratory in Vijayanagara, claiming he had perfected a secret clay crucible that could turn common river sand into pure silver.
Before a gathering of wealthy merchants, he put sand into the crucible, sealed it with wax, heated it in a charcoal furnace, and opened it:
Inside were ten bright, solid silver beads!
The merchants were dazzled, offering thousands of gold coins to buy the 'miraculous crucible'.

Tenali Raman attended the demonstration.
He examined the crucible: it was an ordinary earthenware pot coated with dark red clay slip.
Tenali smiled: 'Master Siddha, your alchemy is magnificent!
Let us perform the trial once more before King Krishnadevaraya in the royal palace, using clay and sand provided by the crown!'

The alchemist, unable to refuse without admitting fraud, arrived at the royal audience hall.
Tenali provided an ordinary clay pot, filled it with river sand from the Tungabhadra, and said:
'Now, Master Siddha, seal this pot with your secret wax and heat it in our furnace!'

The alchemist hesitated, sweating profusely:
'Master Tenali, my alchemy works only in my own consecrated laboratory with my own ancestral crucibles!'

Tenali picked up the alchemist’s original 'miraculous crucible' from the table:
'Then let us examine your ancestral vessel!'
Tenali picked up an iron hammer and cleanly cracked the crucible in two!

He held up the broken pieces before the King:
The clay crucible had a **false bottom**!
Between the double layers of clay, the alchemist had concealed ten real silver beads, sealed with wax that melted when heated, allowing the silver to drop into the sand!

The court erupted in outrage!
King Krishnadevaraya ordered the charlatan arrested and his ill-gotten wealth distributed to the cheated merchants.
Tenali laughed:
'Maharaj, those who promise silver from dirt always have their silver hidden in the false bottoms of their own greed!'
The King rewarded Tenali, once again defending public reason against fraud.
moral: Charlatans who claim secret transmutation cannot withstand the bright light of independent testing.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 147
summary: A corrupt, ambitious courtier named Mallikarjuna sought to remove honest ministers from King Krishnadevaraya’s council. He approached the...
full_text:
A corrupt, ambitious courtier named Mallikarjuna sought to remove honest ministers from King Krishnadevaraya’s council. He approached the King with an ornate signet ring set with a black onyx stone, whispering:
'Maharaj, this is an ancient sacred talisman.
When you wear it on your thumb, it vibrates and whispers warnings whenever a minister in your presence harbors treacherous thoughts!
Yesterday, when Prime Minister Appaji spoke, the ring vibrated fiercely, proving his disloyalty!'

The King, though skeptical, was unsettled by the claim.
Tenali Raman noticed the King’s troubled brow and asked to examine the ring.

Tenali took the ring, slipped it onto his own thumb, and walked up to King Krishnadevaraya.
Tenali closed his eyes, frowned with deep concentration, and suddenly began shaking his hand violently!
'Maharaj! The ring! It is vibrating with furious, uncontrollable intensity! It is buzzing like a hornet’s nest!'

The King stared in alarm: 'What does it whisper, Tenali?'

Tenali shouted in theatrical terror:
'The ring whispers: "Beware! The courtier Mallikarjuna is an insidious traitor who is planning to poison the royal elephant and steal the crown jewels tomorrow midnight!"'

Mallikarjuna turned pale as death, dropping to his knees, screaming:
'Lies! Treason! I never planned such things! The ring is lying!'

Tenali laughed with booming joy, pulling the ring from his thumb:
'Aha, Mallikarjuna! If the ring was telling the truth yesterday about the loyal Prime Minister, why is it lying today about you?
And if it is lying today, it was a fraudulent trick yesterday!'

Tenali examined the inner band of the ring before the King:
Inside the hollow bezel was a tiny, coiled steel spring attached to a minute sliding peg, which the wearer could press with his forefinger to make the stone click and vibrate!

King Krishnadevaraya was furious at the deception.
He stripped Mallikarjuna of all titles, banished him from court, and restored full confidence to his loyal ministers.
The King embraced Tenali:
'Tenali, thy quick wit has broken another insidious chain of courtly intrigue!'
moral: Flattery that claims supernatural signs to influence policy is exposed by silence.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 148
summary: Two traveling grain merchants, Shankara and Ramadas, appeared before the royal magistrate of Vijayanagara, both claiming ownership of a s...
full_text:
Two traveling grain merchants, Shankara and Ramadas, appeared before the royal magistrate of Vijayanagara, both claiming ownership of a sturdy, red wooden bullock cart pulled by two white Kangayam oxen.
Shankara swore: 'I bought the cart in Bellary two months ago; Ramadas stole it while I was eating at an inn!'
Ramadas yelled: 'A lie! I had the cart built by my village carpenter; it is mine!'

Both men produced receipts from different carpenters, and the magistrate was baffled.
Tenali Raman was invited to resolve the dispute.

Tenali inspected the cart and the two white bullocks.
He said: 'Maharaj, paper receipts can be forged, but the memory of animals cannot be bribed.
Let us take the cart to the Great Crossroads outside the city, where four highways branch off to four different provinces.'

The court retinue rode to the four-way crossroads.
Tenali had both merchants stand in the center of the road, fifty paces away from the cart.
Tenali ordered the driver to step down, loosened the reins completely, and placed them loosely upon the oxen's backs.
Tenali clapped his hands: 'Go home, brothers!'

The two white oxen turned their heads, sniffed the air, and without hesitation, turned down the southern road leading toward Ramadas’s village!
The cart trotted for two miles down the highway, turned into a narrow country lane, entered an open village farmhouse courtyard, and walked straight up to the feeding trough, where two young children ran out shouting:
'Father's cart is home!'

Tenali turned to the King and the assembly:
'An animal knows its own stable, its own trough, and the voices of its master's children!
Nature has delivered the verdict!'

Shankara hung his head in shame, confessing that he had stolen the cart from an inn.
The cart and oxen were restored to honest Ramadas, Shankara was fined thirty silver coins, and the people celebrated Tenali Raman’s reliance on the incorruptible truth of nature.
moral: Animals know their own homes; releasing the reins reveals the true master.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 149
summary: A brilliant actor and linguist named Bahurupi Govinda arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he was an absolute master of di...
full_text:
A brilliant actor and linguist named Bahurupi Govinda arrived at the court of Vijayanagara, boasting that he was an absolute master of disguise.
He challenged King Krishnadevaraya:
'Your Majesty! For seven days, I will walk through your court and city in seven different disguises—as a beggar, a merchant, an astrologer, a soldier, a monk, a physician, and a woman.
If your famous wit Tenali Raman cannot unmask me on any day, you must award me five hundred gold coins!'

Tenali accepted the wager.
On the first day, a beggar asked for alms; Tenali looked into his eyes and said: 'Greetings, Govinda!'
On the second day, a physician offered herbs; Tenali unmasked him immediately by his gait.
On the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days, Tenali penetrated every disguise through careful observation.

On the seventh day, a dignified scholar from Kashmir arrived, speaking impeccable classical Kashmiri, wearing authentic northern furs, debating Sanskrit with profound erudition.
The King was convinced this was a real northern scholar, and even Tenali could find no flaw in his accent, clothing, or behavior!
The sun was setting, and the court prepared to declare Govinda victorious.

As the Kashmiri scholar bowed low to the King to conclude the audience, Tenali Raman quietly slipped behind him, holding a small brass vessel of ice-cold mountain spring water.
Without warning, Tenali dumped the freezing water down the back of the scholar’s neck!

The scholar leaped into the air like a scalded cat, clutching his wet neck, and shouted in fluent, unvarnished, colloquial local **Telugu**:
*‘AYYO! AMMA! WHO POURED COLD WATER DOWN MY SHIRT?’*

The entire court erupted in roaring laughter!
Govinda stood soaked and sheepish, realizing that his native tongue had betrayed him!

Tenali smiled with dazzling triumph:
'Maharaj, a man may master ten foreign languages and practice seventy disguises, but when struck by sudden pain or cold water, he always cries out in his mother tongue!'

The actor bowed low, laughing in admiration:
'Tenali Raman, thou art truly invincible! No disguise can deceive thy understanding of human nature!'
The King rewarded both Tenali and the actor for an unforgettable demonstration of psychology and wit.
moral: An actor may change his costume and accent, but his native tongue betrays him in moments of sudden surprise.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 150
summary: King Krishnadevaraya, feeling restless and weary of courtly flattery, summoned Tenali Raman to his private chamber at midnight: 'Tenali, ...
full_text:
King Krishnadevaraya, feeling restless and weary of courtly flattery, summoned Tenali Raman to his private chamber at midnight:
'Tenali, put on the coarse wool cloak of an ordinary night watchman. We shall walk through the sleeping quarters of Vijayanagara to see how our subjects fare when they believe no Emperor watches them.'

The King and Tenali slipped through a secret postern gate into the quiet city.
They walked through the weavers' quarter, where loom lamps burned late as tired mothers finished fabric for the morning market.
In the bakers' lane, they smelled fresh bread being prepared for the hungry porters.
At the city hospital, they observed selfless physicians tending the sick by candlelight without asking for pay.

In a dark alley near the grain market, they encountered a municipal patrol captain shaking down an elderly vegetable vendor, demanding bribes.
Before the King could draw his sword in wrath, Tenali stepped forward in the shadows, raised his heavy wooden night watchman's staff, and shouted in the voice of the Chief Constable:
'Halt! Inspection by the Royal Guard!'
The corrupt captain dropped his loot, took to his heels, and fled into the night!

The grateful vegetable vendor bowed to the two disguised watchmen, handing them two fresh, sweet mangoes:
'Take these, honest brothers; you have protected my family's bread tonight.'

The King accepted the mango with deep reverence, tears glistening in his eyes.
As dawn broke over the Tungabhadra River, King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali on the palace balcony:
'Tenali, tonight I saw the true soul of my empire.
I saw the toil of the weaver, the charity of the physician, the vulnerability of the poor vendor, and the corruption that hides in dark corners.
A ruler who sits only on a golden throne sees only what flatterers want him to see; but he who walks the night with an honest companion sees the living heart of his people.'

The King promoted the selfless physicians, dismissed the corrupt patrol officers, lowered taxes on working weavers, and thanked Tenali Raman for being his eternal compass of truth.
moral: A sovereign who walks among his people learns their real needs, guided by the lantern of honest counsel.

title: Tenali Raman Tale 151
summary: On the twentieth anniversary of King Krishnadevaraya’s coronation, an imperial assembly of poets, scholars, and monarchs from across Bhar...
full_text:
On the twentieth anniversary of King Krishnadevaraya’s coronation, an imperial assembly of poets, scholars, and monarchs from across Bharatavarsha gathered in the Grand Hall of Victory at Vijayanagara.
The royal court poet laureate, Allasani Peddana, stood before the assembly and presented a gold-embroidered crown of pearls to the Emperor, praising his reign as the Golden Age of Literature and Justice.

King Krishnadevaraya took the pearl crown in his hands.
He did not place it upon his own head.
The Emperor stood up from his Golden Throne, walked down the marble steps into the center of the hall, and approached Tenali Raman!

The court watched in breathless silence.
King Krishnadevaraya placed the pearl crown upon Tenali Raman’s head, and proclaimed before the entire empire:
'Scholars and kings of Bharatavarsha!
Many emperors have armies, fortresses, and treasuries of diamonds.
But the greatest treasure of Vijayanagara has been our *Vikatakavi*—Tenali Raman!

When flattery blinded my eyes, his wit gave me sight.
When anger inflamed my sword, his humor poured cooling water upon my heart.
When corruption oppressed the poor, his courage held up the mirror of justice before power.
He never flattered a monarch for gold, nor did he ever despise a humble beggar.
His laughter was the shield of the innocent, his poetry was the music of truth, and his wisdom preserved the soul of our empire!'

Tenali Raman bowed low, tears of profound emotion in his eyes.
He took off the pearl crown and placed it gently at the Emperor’s feet:
'Maharaj, a crown belongs on the head of a righteous king who loves his people.
My only crown is the joy of our citizens, the laughter in your halls, and the truth that unites our hearts.'

The entire assembly of ten thousand dignitaries, soldiers, and citizens erupted in thunderous, standing applause that echoed across the Tungabhadra River and down the corridors of history.
And so the legend of Tenali Raman lived on for centuries—remembered not merely as a jester who made a king laugh, but as the eternal poet of wisdom, courage, and righteous wit who proved that a single honest laugh can illuminate the darkest world.
moral: The true jester does not merely provoke laughter; he wields wit as the shield of justice, the sword of truth, and the soul of wisdom.
